title: Subcellular Optogenetic Control of PI(4,5)P2 in Insulin-Secreting Cells: Molecular Engineering and Implementation.
abstract: PI(4,5)P2 plays a crucial role in distinct cell signalling. Traditional methods, such as genetic knockout/overexpression and pharmacological tools, are useful but lack high spatiotemporal resolution, which is often required to recapitulate endogenous dynamics and specificity of lipid signaling. To overcome these problems, we have developed the optical genetic method, enabling rapid manipulation of PI(4,5)P2 at subcellular loci. It utilizes light as a trigger to bypass constraints of traditional interventions to directly investigate acute spatially defined PI(4,5)P2 signaling. Distinct pairs of light-inducible dimerization proteins, including improved light-inducible dimers (iLID)/Micro and cryptochrome 2 (CRY2)/CIBN (CIB1 truncation), were used. One part of the dimer carries the 5'-phosphatase domain (5'Ptase) of oculocerebrorenal syndrome of Lowe protein (OCRL), and the other part carries an anchor sequence that resides at a specific loci of interest in the cells. This unique approach makes it possible to rapidly manipulate PI(4,5)P2 levels within ~120 nm nanodomains of insulin granule docking sites on the plasma membrane, revealing an essential role of local (PI(4,5)P2) metabolism to control granule tethering and docking, which is distinct from its known function in the steps of vesicle priming and vesicle fusion. The approach allows investigating time-sensitive and site-specific phosphoinositide signaling in membrane trafficking.

title: Super-Resolution Imaging of PI(4,5)P2 and Other Phosphoinositides in the Cell Plasma Membrane with PALM and dSTORM.
abstract: Phosphoinositides comprise a small fraction of membrane phospholipids yet exert fundamental control over cellular function by organizing signaling and membrane dynamics. They define organelle identity, spatially restrict intracellular signaling, and coordinate membrane trafficking and protein activity. Disruption of their metabolism contributes to cancer, diabetes, and neurodegeneration. Among the seven species, phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PtdIns(4,5)P2 or PI(4,5)P2) is the most abundant phosphoinositide at the plasma membrane, and it functions both as a precursor for phospholipase C-mediated generation of diacylglycerol and inositol-1,4,5 trisphosphate (IP3) and as a direct regulator of numerous effector proteins controlling vesicle trafficking, cytoskeleton dynamics, ion channels, and transporters. To resolve its nanoscale organization, we developed a single-molecule super-resolution imaging approach using PALM and dSTORM imaging combined with new dual-color fluorescent probes based on the PLCδ1 pleckstrin homology domain. Nanoscale quantitative mapping reveals that PtdIns(4,5)P₂ is diffusely distributed across flat plasma membrane regions, with only modest enrichment in small patches preferentially localized at the curved regions, cell edges, and protrusions. Dense nanodomains are detected only with traditional fixation but not under optimized fixation or in live cells. The results support a model in which a predominant diffusive pool of PtdIns(4,5)P₂ coexists with spatially restricted equilibrating sites of local synthesis, rather than stable high-gradient nanoclusters. This approach can be extended to image other phosphoinositide species by changing the probe.

title: Force and Power Testing in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Literature: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Force and power testing has been recognised as a key aspect of anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) rehabilitation. However, a literature synthesis is required to examine how these physical characteristics have been assessed due to pronounced heterogeneity in the methods used. To synthesise and describe the existing literature on force and power testing post-ACLR. A scoping review of the electronic databases MEDLINE (PubMed), SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library and PEDro was conducted including studies adopting at least one force or power test in patients post-ACLR. The search methodology followed the Joanna Briggs Institute Manual for evidence synthesis and included the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). In total, 1625 studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria. Seven main device categories were identified, with different rates of implementation over the years (1981-2023) and throughout the recovery process: (1) isokinetic dynamometry (IKD; 64.9%), (2) jump (without force platform; 32.2%), (3) force platform (28.0%), (4) traditional gym equipment and bodyweight exercises (6.2%), (5) hand-held dynamometry (4.0%), (6) manual muscle testing (1.5%) and (7) other devices (5.5%). Studies used 1.42 ± 0.62 devices, with 45 different combinations recorded. Various tests were conducted using different devices, ranging from 8 to 72 recorded tests per category. Only force plate assessments showed a linear increment in implementation from the surgical procedure (r = 0.86, p = 0.012). Significant heterogeneity in assessment device selection, metrics analysed, test implementation and protocols was observed. Most studies included a single device category to examine force and power characteristics of patients post-ACLR. The IKD remains the most adopted testing device in research, but current assessment practices are more varied than in the past.

title: The immune microenvironment of solid tumor leptomeningeal metastasis: pathways, characteristics and therapies.
abstract: Meningeal metastasis refers to the spread of cancer cells from the primary tumor to the dura mater or pia mater, often accompanied by the dissemination of tumor cells into the cerebrospinal fluid. Our review mainly focuses on leptomeningeal metastasis. The presence of leptomeningeal metastasis typically signifies advanced disease stage and is associated with poor prognosis. Although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear, elucidating the relevant signaling pathways is critical for understanding the disease process and developing effective interventions. Accumulating evidence has highlighted the potential of targeted therapies and immune checkpoint inhibitors for the treatment of leptomeningeal metastasis. However, their clinical efficacy remains limited owing to the restrictive nature of the blood-brain barrier and the distinct immune microenvironment of the meninges. Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of the tumor microenvironment in leptomeningeal metastasis is urgently required. In addition, we summarize monotherapy and combination therapeutic strategies targeting the tumor microenvironment, along with the design and outcomes of relevant clinical trials. Finally, this review aimed to systematically summarize the key signaling pathways and tumor microenvironment components involved in leptomeningeal metastasis, with particular emphasis on the contrasting roles of protumor and antitumor immune microenvironments, to provide a theoretical foundation for the development of precise therapeutic strategies.

title: From Reactive Care to Prevention in Neurodegenerative Diseases: Biomarkers, Risk Prediction, and Early Intervention.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) are typically diagnosed only after substantial and irreversible neuronal damage has occurred, at a point when disease-modifying interventions are least likely to be effective. Increasing evidence indicates that the molecular and cellular processes driving neurodegeneration often begin years to decades before clinical onset. This preclinical phase offers an opportunity for early detection, although translating it into clinically effective prevention remains a major challenge. In this review, we examine advances in fluid-based, neuroimaging, genetic, and multi-omics biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, and other NDs. We propose a staged framework, from risk prediction to actionable intervention, to discuss how integrating these biomarkers may improve early diagnosis and risk assessment and guide interventions aimed at delaying or preventing disease onset. Finally, we discuss emerging prevention-oriented clinical trials, the potential and limitations of artificial intelligence-based prediction, and the ethical implications of moving neurological care from reactive management to predictive and preventive medicine.

title: Clinical, Genetic, MR Spectroscopy characteristics and Response to Flunarizine in Episodic Ataxia Type 2: The Sheffield Ataxia Cohort.
abstract: Episodic ataxia type 2 (EA2) is an autosomal-dominant calcium channelopathy caused by pathogenic mutations in the CACNA1A gene, characterized by episodic cerebellar symptoms and marked phenotypic heterogeneity. Data on real-world clinical features and treatment responses, particularly in the era of major genetic advances, remain limited. This is a retrospective observational single-centre case series of 58 individuals from 38 families with genetically confirmed EA2. Clinical, demographic, genetic, and treatment data were extracted from medical records using a standardized Excel-based data collection tool. Symptom patterns with associated neurological features, genetic characteristics, and treatment responses were analyzed descriptively. Paired MRI imaging including MR spectroscopy (MRS) of the cerebellum at baseline and follow up data, and medication efficacy were assessed using patient-reported benefit, and statistical analysis was performed using Wilcoxon signed rank test and Exact binomial testing respectively. The mean age at diagnosis was 35.2 ± 21.5 years, and a positive family history was identified in 48 patients (82.70%). The most frequent clinical manifestations were gait instability (87.93%), dysarthria (39.66%), headache (58.62%) and isolated dizziness (48.28%). Episodic symptoms predominated, with 33 patients (56.89%) experiencing discrete attacks. Amongst those with episodic symptoms, weekly attacks were the most common (42.4%), while 17 patients (29.31%) exhibited a non-episodic course with persistent symptoms. Interictal oculomotor abnormalities, including nystagmus, were noted in some individuals. Paired longitudinal MRS analyses for both vermis (W = 118.0, p = 0.67) and hemisphere (W = 122.0, p = 0.39) revealed no significant change over time. Flunarizine showed the highest rate of therapeutic benefit, with 76.5% of treated patients reporting improvement (p = 0.04), whereas other treatments demonstrated variable but non-significant effects. This study highlights the clinical heterogeneity and neuroimaging (MRS) insight of EA2 underscoring the predominance of episodic manifestations, while also recognizing a subset with non-episodic symptoms. Flunarizine appears to be an effective, accessible therapeutic option for reducing attack frequency and duration in EA2, though further studies are required to compare efficacy with alternative therapeutic options such as acetazolamide.

Despite growing interest in investigating microstructure using GWC, its relationship to cell type-related tissue properties is understudied. We leverage spatially resolved post-mortem transcriptomic data from six donors to identify associations between cell type marker genes and GWC averaged across cognitively normal living adults ([Formula: see text] = 577, mean age = 56.2 years). title: Piracetam modulates secondary injury responses and neuroplasticity-related alterations after mild traumatic brain injury.
abstract: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) initiates secondary inflammatory, oxidative, apoptotic, and synaptic alterations that may contribute to persistent cognitive and affective dysfunction. This study investigated the effects of post-injury piracetam treatment in a rat model of mTBI. Twenty-one male Wistar rats were randomly assigned to control (CON), mild brain trauma (mBT), and piracetam-treated (PT) groups (n = 7 each). Piracetam (200 mg/kg, i.p.) was administered 1 h after injury. Locomotor, anxiety-related, depression-related, and recognition-memory outcomes were assessed using the open field, elevated plus maze, forced swim, and novel object recognition tests. Hippocampal and plasma TNF-α, COX-2, caspase-3, total antioxidant status, total oxidant status, oxidative stress index, BDNF, and AChE were measured, together with histopathological and immunohistochemical evaluation of the cortex, CA3, and dentate gyrus. mTBI impaired anxiety-related, depression-related, and recognition-memory measures without altering locomotor activity and was accompanied by inflammatory, oxidative, apoptosis-associated, neurotrophic, and cholinergic-related alterations. Piracetam significantly attenuated these behavioral and biochemical changes and shifted most parameters toward control levels. Histopathological improvement was partial and region-dependent, with the most consistent effects observed in the CA3 region. Piracetam reduced GFAP and CD68 immunoreactivity and increased synaptophysin immunoreactivity relative to the mild brain trauma (mBT) group. VEGF immunoreactivity did not differ significantly between the piracetam-treated and mBT groups after correction for multiple comparisons. These findings suggest that a single post-injury dose of piracetam attenuated several secondary injury responses in this rat model of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). The results warrant further preclinical investigation.

title: Theory of mind, autism-like traits, executive functions, and structural brain MRI findings in children with neurofibromatosis type 1.
abstract: This study aimed to examine social-cognitive difficulties in children with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) by jointly investigating theory of mind (ToM), executive functions, and autism-like traits and to explore whether children with NF1 show structural differences in brain regions commonly implicated in social cognition and executive functioning. In this two-center cross-sectional study, 41 children aged 8-18 years were included, comprising 21 children with NF1 and 20 age- and sex-matched typically developing children. Participants underwent behavioral assessment, including parent-reported autism-like traits, everyday executive functioning, and direct measures of ToM. Structural brain MRI data were analyzed using automated volumetric and cortical thickness measures, focusing on these regions. Children with NF1 showed higher autism-like traits, lower everyday executive functioning in play and social routines, and poorer performance on an advanced ToM task. The NF1 group also had larger global brain volume reflecting widespread white matter expansion; lower cortical gray matter proportion and thickness in frontal, temporal, parietal, cingulate, and limbic regions; and larger subcortical structures including the amygdala, hippocampus, and thalamus. Exploratory within-group brain-behavior correlations were few and selective, none survived multiple-comparison correction, and none involved autism-like traits. Children with NF1 display a multidimensional profile of social-cognitive difficulties together with structural differences indicating an imbalance between cortical and subcortical regions typically involved in social cognition. These structural differences offer a possible neurobiological substrate for the social-cognitive difficulties observed in NF1. Whether they account for these difficulties remains to be tested in samples powered to examine brain-behavior associations directly. • Children with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) frequently show executive dysfunction, autism-like traits, and theory of mind (ToM) difficulties. • These domains have rarely been examined jointly, or alongside brain structure, in the same children. • Autism-like traits, everyday executive difficulties, and poorer ToM co-occurred in children with NF1. • The same children showed reduced cortical thickness and proportion with enlarged subcortical structures in regions implicated in social cognition, a candidate substrate for future brain-behavior studies.

title: Cognitive impairment profiles and their cerebellar structural correlates in spinocerebellar ataxia type 3: a CANTAB-based study.
abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), the most common hereditary ataxia, exhibits characteristic cerebellar-related cognitive impairment owing to its relatively focal cerebellar pathology. To investigate the characteristics of cognitive impairment in SCA3 patients and its correlation with cerebellar structure. The study included 42 SCA3 patients and 17 healthy controls. The patients were divided into mild (SARA < 8, n = 12) and moderate-to-severe (SARA ≥ 8, n = 30) groups based on Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia, as well as cognitive-preserved (MoCA ≥ 26, n = 23) and cognitively impaired (MoCA < 26, n = 19) groups based on Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Cognitive function and cerebellar regional volumes were compared. The Bootstrap method and Pearson correlation analysis were used to examine the mediating effect of cerebellar structural changes on cognitive impairment and their associations. Compared with healthy controls, SCA3 patients exhibited impairments in executive function, visual working memory, spatial planning ability, and spatial working memory. Compared with patients with mild ataxia, those with moderate-to-severe ataxia showed impaired visual working memory, poorer planning of complex tasks, and lower task accuracy. Increased average processing time was observed in patients with preserved cognition, while impaired 0-s delayed response was observed only in patients with cognitive impairment. The Left_Crus Ⅰ region of the cerebellum exerts a protective effect on the age of onset as measured by the spatial planning strategies; the Left_Ⅸ and Right_Ⅹ regions are associated with spatial planning and executive function; and the Left_Crus Ⅰ and Bilateral_Ⅸ regions, among others, are associated with visual working memory and executive function. Patients with SCA3 exhibit multifaceted cognitive impairments that are associated with specific cerebellar lobules.

title: Molecular chaperones involved in the radiobiological response of established triple-negative breast cancer cell lines: a pilot study.
abstract: Radiation therapy (RT) represents a key component of the multimodal treatment of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), however, radioresistance remains a significant clinical challenge often driven by dysregulated stress-response and survival signaling pathways. Because the efficacy of RT is strongly dependent on the intrinsic biological features of distinct tumor subtypes, including TNBC, the investigation of the molecular determinants of radiosensitivity is crucial to develop biology-driven personalized RT protocols. In this study, the radiobiological response of three established TNBC cell lines (MDA-MB-231, SUM-159, and BT-549) exposed to increasing X-ray doses (1-5 Gy) was evaluated. Radiation survival curves were analyzed using the linear-quadratic (LQ) model to estimate the intrinsic α and β radiosensitivity parameters. To investigate stress-mediated molecular mechanisms underlying radioresistence, cellular responses to 5 Gy radiation were analyzed by assessing heat shock protein expression Hsp27, Hsp60, and Hsp90- via Western blot and Immunofluorescence. Furthermore, downstream alterations in key oncogenic and DNA damage response pathways including p53, Akt, 53BP1, survivin, and JNK, were characterized across all models. We observed variability in the expression profiles of the target proteins among the three TNBC cell lines, potentially reflecting differences in their estimated radiobiological features.We predict that appropriately validated, biomarker-directed therapies are more likely to be successfully integrated into precision medicine strategies for hard-to-treat tumors.

title: Familial ACOX1-related neurodegeneration with progressive demyelination: Clinical and NODDI findings in two siblings.
abstract: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in the ACOX1 gene result in neuronal loss due to peroxisomal disorder and elevated very long chain fatty acids (VLCFA). On the other hand, a recurrent monoallelic gain-of-function variant (p.N237S) in ACOX1 has been associated with neurodegeneration, skin rash, hearing loss, and peripheral neuropathy, a condition known as Mitchell syndrome. Herein, we report on two siblings with ataxia, cognitive decline, progressive demyelination, and normal VLCFA who share a missense variant in the ACOX1 gene (p.R490G) in heterozygosis inherited from their clinically asymptomatic mother. Brain MRI showed progressive demyelination and callosal hypoplasia. Neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) analyses showed that the probands' intraneurite fraction is smaller than that of their parents. Also, the orientation dispersion index in the probands was smaller. These results show that diffusion MRI microstructure modeling may be a useful tool for diagnosis and follow-up of hypomyelinating conditions.

title: Effects of Palmitoylethanolamide on the Retinal Endocannabinoid System in Amyloidosis Mice.
journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology
abstract: Recently, we demonstrated the dysregulation of the endocannabinoid (eCB) system (ECS) in the retinas of Alzheimer's disease (AD)-like mice. Here, we explored the impact of the eCB-like lipid palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) on the retinal ECS of the Tg2576 (TG) mouse model of amyloidosis. Chronic subcutaneous administration of PEA via implanted micro-pellets was associated with the up-regulation of cannabinoid receptor 2 (CB2) and the modulation of the two eCB metabolic enzymes Diacylglycerol-lipase β (DAGL-β) and monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL). Intriguingly, these effects were restricted to TG mice and were absent in wild-type animals, pointing to a condition-dependent modulation of the retinal ECS by PEA. Additionally, a distinctive nuclear CB2 signal consistent with nuclear localization was observed in the ganglion cell layer of TG retinas, a finding independent of PEA treatment. Taken together, our data provide novel insights into the PEA-associated biochemical modulation of the retinal ECS in a model of amyloidosis.

title: Radial Pressure Wave Therapy Attenuates Chronic Postoperative Pain via Spinal CB1/CB2 Receptors and Is Associated With Increased 2-AG Levels.
abstract: Radial pressure wave therapy (RPWT) has shown analgesic effects in musculoskeletal disorders; however, the central mechanisms underlying its antinociceptive actions remain poorly characterized. Here, we investigated the contribution of spinal endocannabinoid system (ECS) signalling to RPWT-induced antinociception in a murine model of CPOP. Male C57BL/6 mice underwent skin and muscle incision/retraction of the right thigh to induce persistent postoperative pain. Mechanical hypersensitivity was assessed using von Frey filaments. RPWT was applied on postoperative days 14 and 16. To determine the involvement of spinal ECS signalling, CB1 and CB2 receptor inverse agonists (AM251 and AM630), as well as inhibitors of endocannabinoid reuptake and degradation, were administered intrathecally before RPWT. Spinal expression of cannabinoid receptors and endocannabinoid metabolic enzymes was evaluated by Western blotting. Spinal cytokine levels were measured by ELISA, and concentrations of anandamide (AEA) and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) were quantified. RPWT significantly reduced CPOP-induced mechanical hypersensitivity, with the greatest antinociceptive effect observed at 100 pulses. Pharmacological blockade of CB1 or CB2 receptors abolished RPWT-induced antinociception, supporting a receptor-dependent mechanism. Inhibition of endocannabinoid reuptake and degradation further enhanced RPWT-induced analgesia. Additionally, RPWT reduced spinal monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL) protein expression, increased spinal 2-AG levels and decreased spinal IL-1β levels compared with untreated CPOP mice. Together, these findings demonstrate that RPWT transiently attenuates mechanical hypersensitivity in a mouse model of chronic postoperative pain through mechanisms requiring spinal CB1 and CB2 receptor signalling. This antinociceptive effect is associated with increased spinal 2-AG levels and reduced MAGL expression, suggesting a potential involvement of the spinal endocannabinoid system.

title: A comparison of data reduction approaches for the identification of non-cognitive symptom subsyndromes in Alzheimer's disease, based on Neuropsychiatric Inventory scores.
abstract: BackgroundWithin Alzheimer's disease, attempts to perform data reduction on the non-cognitive symptoms comprising the Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI) have been inconsistent. Here, most studies used principal component analysis (PCA), despite reports that exploratory factor analysis (EFA) estimates loadings more accurately.ObjectiveWe compared how well different data reduction approaches derived NPI models in a discovery dataset (Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, n = 460), based on confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in two independent datasets (Brains for Dementia Research, n = 337 and Memento, n = 211). Specifically, we assessed PCA, maximum likelihood (ML) EFA, principal axis (PA) EFA, and a PCA extension that adjusts for zero inflation. For each method, we additionally compared how different approaches to determine the number of factors/components affected CFA fit indices.MethodsEFA and standard PCA were performed using PSYCH, the zero-inflation adjusted PCA using zibppca, and CFA was performed in Lavaan (all R packages).ResultsIn both confirmatory datasets, PA EFA yielded the closest fitting model (Tucker Lewis Index > 0.95). This model comprised [agitation and irritability], [depression and anxiety], [delusions and hallucinations], and [elation and disinhibition]. We also demonstrated that selecting the number of latent constructs to retain using parallel analysis based on null factors, as opposed to component eigenvalues, was necessary to identify this best fitting model.ConclusionsPA EFA allowed the identification of an acceptable CFA verified NPI subsyndrome structure. Our findings also indicate that previous attempts to identify NPI subsyndrome structure might have been hindered by extracting too few factors/components.

title: TToTP model: An automated detection of Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia using Tesla Tree of Thought Pattern with EEG signals.
abstract: BackgroundAlzheimer's disease (AD) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are common neurological disorders.Objective:To facilitate the early detection of these conditions, we aimed to propose a new self-organized explainable feature engineering (SOXFE) model. Additionally, we sought to investigate the feature extraction capabilities.MethodsWe used a publicly available electroencephalography (EEG) dementia detection dataset. This dataset was created to collect EEG signals from participants in three categories: (i) AD, (ii) FTD, and (iii) healthy control (HC). To automatically detect these groups, we proposed a new SOXFE model. This model includes a novel feature extraction function inspired by Tesla's 369 vortex and the Tree of Thought (ToT), termed the Tesla Tree of Thought Pattern (TToTP). In the feature selection phase, we applied cumulative weighted iterative neighborhood component analysis (CWINCA), to select the most informative features. In the classification phase, we employed the t algorithm-based k-nearest neighbors (tkNN). The fourth phase involves information fusion, where the results from each channel are voted on using iterative majority voting (IMV), and the best outcome is selected. The final phase is explainable results generation, in which a cortical channel map (CCMap) is created based on the findings from the information fusion phase.ResultsWe applied the TToTP-based SOXFE model to the EEG dementia dataset, achieving over 99% classification accuracy. Additionally, a cortical channel map was generated using the classification results.ConclusionsThe proposed TToTP-based SOXFE model achieved high classification performance and successfully generated a cortical channel map. The model contributes to both feature engineering and neuroscience.

title: The Clinical and Neuro-Informed Benefits of Utilizing a Grief-Focused Camp for Supporting Childhood Bereavement.
abstract: Grief-focused camps offer clinical and neuro-informed benefits for grieving children. This conceptual article highlights both design and implementation of a bereavement camp, exploring how structured, experiential, and expressive activities engage developing neural networks involved in emotion regulation, attachment, and stress response. Drawing on the Dual-Processing Model of Grief and the Window of Tolerance, the camp model emphasizes relational safety, peer normalization, and multisensory engagement to promote adaptive coping and support the grieving processes. Rotating small-group sessions, large-group activities, and ending with guardian-inclusive activities provides repeated corrective emotional experiences supporting neuroplasticity and resilience. The design intentionally balances opportunities for processing loss with restorative, play-based experiences fostering emotional growth and co-regulation. Clinical implications for counselors include program and staff structures and supervision, grounded in neuro-informed principles. By applying a neuroscience lens to grief-focused camp design, this model demonstrates potential to enhance coping, emotional development, and long-term adaptive functioning in bereaved children.

title: Cerebellar optogenetic stimulation restores motor cortex activity and behaviour after stroke.
abstract: Stroke causes severe motor deficits, but functional recovery can occur through neural circuit reorganization in areas adjacent to and remote from the infarct. Optogenetic stimulation can modulate neuronal activity and improve recovery in experimental models, yet the population-level cortical dynamics underlying these effects remain poorly understood. The lateral cerebellar nucleus projects to the cortex via the dentatothalamocortical pathway and represents a promising target for remote neuromodulation after stroke. We performed longitudinal one-photon calcium imaging of ipsilesional primary motor cortex layer V neurons in awake, behaving mice (n = 13) following transient middle cerebral artery occlusion. Mice received optogenetic stimulation of the contralesional lateral cerebellar nucleus using CaMKII-driven Channelrhodopsin-2 on post-stroke days 5 through 14. Stimulation-treated and non-stimulated stroke mice were compared across behavioral and neural activity measures for up to 28 days post-stroke. Stroke significantly reduced ipsilesional motor cortex population activity during the subacute phase, with decreased calcium peak frequency (p < 0.001) and amplitude (p = 0.004). Reduced frequency was strongly associated with lesion size at post-stroke day 6 (r² = 0.88, p < 0.001), and reduced amplitude was similarly associated with lesion size at post-stroke day 9 (r² = 0.39, p = 0.022). Cerebellar stimulation counteracted these deficits, significantly increasing both frequency (p = 0.017) and amplitude (p < 0.001) and improving behavioral recovery on the rotating beam task (p = 0.027). Critically, in stimulated animals, motor cortex activity was no longer coupled to lesion size, indicating that stimulation decoupled cortical dynamics from injury severity. Early post-stroke functional connection density among motor cortex neurons predicted long-term behavioral outcome in non-stimulated animals (r² = 0.50, p = 0.033), but this relationship was abolished by stimulation, suggesting that cerebellar stimulation reshaped the recovery trajectory independently of initial network disruption. Stroke also shifted neuronal populations toward minimally active states, and stimulation preserved a higher proportion of moderately active neurons (p = 0.029). These findings define population-level changes in peri-lesional motor cortex after stroke at cellular resolution and demonstrate that cerebellar optogenetic stimulation counteracts stroke-induced cortical dysfunction, decouples recovery from lesion burden, and promotes functional recovery.

title: Burnout, Lack of Sleep and the Resulting Reduced Clinical Performance of Neurologists are a Global Problem.
Factors Influencing Publication Impact in Clinical Neuromuscular Disorders: A Bibliometric Analysis.
abstract: Bibliometric analysis provides an objective method to evaluate trends and patterns. Clinical neuromuscular medicine has evolved rapidly with advances in diagnostics, targeted therapies, and multidisciplinary care. Identifying the most influential research helps assess scientific impact and guide future directions. We performed a bibliometric analysis of the 50 most-cited articles in clinical neuromuscular using the Web of Science Core Collection. We evaluated citation metrics, study design, subspecialties, journal impact factor, funding source, and international collaborations. Data were retrieved through structured search strategies using Boolean operators. Analyses included performance metrics, network mapping, and regression and correlation testing. The literature demonstrates a marked shift toward high-impact therapeutic research. Citation velocity correlated strongly with publication year (r = 0.52, p < 0.001). Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), myasthenia gravis, and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) were the leading topics. Clinical guidelines and consensus statements ranked among the most cited works, with SMA publications achieving the highest citation density (79.5 citations/year), highlighting the transformative effect of disease-modifying therapies. International collaboration significantly predicted impact, with multi-country studies achieving 65% higher citation rates. Industry-funded trials comprised 20% of top-cited articles and demonstrated high citation density. High-impact neurology and general medicine journals published most articles, though journal impact factor showed minimal correlation with citation performance. Disease-modifying therapies are reshaping neuromuscular care. Sustained international collaboration, patient-centered outcomes, and rigorous trial design remain essential to maximize global clinical impact.

title: Neuroinflammation as a Unifying Mechanism in Major Psychiatric Disorders: From Molecular Pathways to Clinical Implications: A Systematic Search and Review.
abstract: To examine whether neuroinflammation can be understood as a unifying mechanism in major psychiatric disorders and summarized its molecular and clinical relevance. Major psychiatric disorders, including major depressive disorder (MDD), bipolar disorder (BD), and schizophrenia, are increasingly linked with immune dysregulation and inflammatory signaling. Neuroinflammation may help explain shared biological mechanisms across these disorders, but the available evidence remains diverse and clinically heterogeneous. This review followed PRISMA 2020 guidance. Electronic searches were conducted in PubMed, ScienceDirect, Cochrane Library, PubMed Central, and Embase for studies published between 2021 and 2026. Only English-language, human studies published between 2021 and 2026 were included. Studies had to address neuroinflammation or related neuroimmune mechanisms in depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, or psychosis. Methodological quality was assessed using design-specific appraisal tools. All 2288 records were identified. 52 duplicates were removed; 2236 records were screened. Twenty-one full text reports were assessed for eligibility, and 15 studies were included in the final synthesis after exclusion of six full-text reports, including one study with high risk of bias. The included studies covered major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, first-episode psychosis, perinatal depression, perimenopausal depression, and cross-diagnostic postmortem datasets. Across these studies, neuroinflammatory involvement was reported through altered cytokines, complement proteins, matrix metalloproteinases, kynurenine-pathway metabolites, immune-cell changes, viral immune associations, and transcriptomic immune pathways. Some intervention studies also showed that symptom improvement was accompanied by favorable changes in inflammatory measures. The available evidence supports an important but heterogeneous role of neuroinflammation across major psychiatric disorders. Current findings suggest shared immune-related mechanisms, but no single biomarker is sufficient as a universal diagnostic marker. Larger and better-designed studies are needed to clarify clinical relevance and therapeutic potential.

title: Diagnostic Utility of the Central Vein Sign in Multiple Sclerosis With Implementation of the 6 Lesion Rule.
abstract: To evaluate the diagnostic value of the central vein sign (CVS) using specific magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequences, such as susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) and gradient echo sequence (GRE), while also assessing its association with cardiovascular risk factors. The central vein sign is a radiological biomarker proposed as a differentiating tool between multiple sclerosis (MS) and nonspecific white matter diseases (WMD), addressing the high rate of MS misdiagnosis. In this case-control study, investigators who were blinded to patients' clinical and demographic data reviewed the brain MRI scans of 598 consecutive patients between January 2016 and August 2022 for the occurrence of the CVS. A total of 422 participants were included after excluding 176 patients. In total, 5939 brain lesions were analyzed: 4773 in 245 patients with MS and 1166 in 177 patients with other WMDs. In patients with MS, the CVS was detected in 1300 lesions (27.23%). The specificity of the 3- and 6-CVS lesion criteria was 89.8% and 100%, respectively. In the multivariate regression model, hypertension and the onset of optic neuritis were independently and negatively associated with the CVS. This study demonstrates that the CVS is highly specific in differentiating MS from other WMDs, suggesting that its integration into the MS diagnostic criteria could enhance MS diagnosis and improve patient outcomes.

title: Clinical and Genetic Characterization of Pediatric Dopa-Responsive Dystonia in Saudi Arabia: A Tertiary Care Cohort Study.
abstract: To describe the clinical and genetic characteristics of pediatric dopa-responsive dystonia (DRD) and evaluate genotype-phenotype correlations and levodopa response in a Saudi tertiary center. This retrospective cohort study included children aged 0-14 years with genetically confirmed DRD evaluated at a tertiary center in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, between 2015 and 2026. Demographic, clinical, genetic, and treatment-related data were collected and analyzed. Dystonia severity before and after treatment was assessed using the Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Rating Scale. Twenty patients were analyzed, and the most commonly affected gene was 6-pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase (PTS) (60.0%). Significant associations were identified between genotype and both dystonia pattern (p = 0.002) and age at onset (p = 0.004). Misdiagnosis rates differed significantly between genetic subgroups (p = 0.023). Most patients showed favorable response to levodopa, although treatment response did not differ significantly between genotypes (p = 0.292). This study highlights the clinical and genetic heterogeneity of pediatric DRD and emphasizes the importance of early recognition and timely levodopa initiation to improve outcomes. Further multicenter studies are needed to better characterize genotype-phenotype correlations and long-term outcomes in pediatric DRD.

title: Evaluating the Role of Visceral Adiposity in Neurological Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Neurological disorders represent a major global health challenge. According to recent Global Burden of Disease (GBD) estimates, Alzheimer's disease and other dementias, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, and headache disorders together account for nearly 3% of the worldwide disease burden. While visceral adipose tissue has traditionally been viewed as a metabolic concern, emerging evidence highlights visceral adiposity as an independent risk factor and potential contributor to the pathogenesis and progression of several neurological disorders. This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines to evaluate the association between visceral adiposity and neurological disorders. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251083846). A comprehensive search of PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science was performed in June 2025. Eligibility criteria were defined using the PICOS framework. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), adapted for cross-sectional designs where applicable. Adjusted effect estimates were pooled using a random-effects model. A total of 26 studies involving 1, 059, 075 participants were included; approximately 96% of participants were female, largely because of one nationwide female-only cohort, and mean ages ranged from 44.5 to 78.3 years. Twenty-three studies (88.5%) reported at least one adverse association between greater visceral or central adiposity and poorer neurological or cognitive outcomes.The meta-analysis of 12 studies showed that elevated visceral adiposity was associated with a 48% higher likelihood of adverse neurological outcomes (pooled effect estimate [OR/HR] = 1.48, 95% CI: 1.27-1.72, p < 0.001; I2 = 83%). Significant associations were observed for stroke-related outcomes (OR = 1.41, 95% CI: 1.15-1.74), young-onset dementia (HR = 1.55, 95% CI: 1.34-1.79), and migraine (OR = 1.41, 95% CI: 1.05-1.88), whereas the pooled estimate for subclinical cerebrovascular imaging findings was elevated but imprecise (OR = 3.49, 95% CI: 0.64-19.10). Elevated visceral adiposity is associated with a higher risk of stroke-related outcomes, dementia, migraine, and adverse brain imaging findings. Given the substantial heterogeneity and the predominance of cross-sectional data, these findings should be confirmed in prospective studies using standardized measures of visceral fat; nevertheless, they support the incorporation of visceral fat assessment into neurological disease prevention strategies.

title: Nociceptive stimulation modulates spinal beta oscillations in awake human epidural recordings.
abstract: Nociceptive processing in the human spinal cord remains difficult to study directly, and its oscillatory dynamics are poorly understood. Oscillatory activity in the beta band (13-35 Hz) is of particular interest, as beta suppression accompanies sensory, including nociceptive, processing in supraspinal networks and may reflect transient network reorganisation. To determine whether temporally precise nociceptive stimulation modulates beta-band activity detectable in human epidural spinal field potentials (eSFPs). In this proof-of-concept study, we recorded eSFPs during experimental noxious laser stimulation of the unaffected foot using externalised thoracic spinal cord stimulation electrodes in 2 subjects undergoing a clinically indicated stimulation trial for neuropathic pain (persistent spinal pain syndrome type 2). Time-frequency responses were assessed using within-subject cluster-based permutation testing. Both subjects showed early suppression of spinal beta activity (13-35 Hz) following nociceptive stimulation. Suppression formed contiguous rostrocaudal clusters and was most prominent within 0 to 200 milliseconds after stimulation. Low-beta (13-20 Hz) suppression predominated rostrally, whereas high-beta (20-35 Hz) suppression was more spatially extensive. These effects were observed across bipolar referencing schemes and analytic constraints. Intertrial coherence was modest and not consistently aligned with early beta suppression, a pattern consistent with induced desynchronisation, although partial phase-reset contributions cannot be excluded. These preliminary findings demonstrate the feasibility of detecting rapid, spatially organised beta-band modulation following nociceptive stimulation using eSFP recordings in awake humans. Larger studies are required to establish the reproducibility, physiological specificity, and potential translational relevance of these spinal oscillatory responses.

title: Brain network overlap as a predictor of depressive symptoms.
abstract: The brain's network architecture supports emotion and cognition and is disrupted in mental disorders, including major depressive disorder. Traditional network models often assign each brain region to a single dominant network. However, accumulating evidence supports an overlapping organization in which regions participate in several networks. Here, we tested whether network overlap (i) is altered in major depressive disorder, (ii) is modulated by a dopaminergic pharmacological challenge and (iii) predicts depressive symptoms. To this end, we evaluated 111 unmedicated individuals (ages: 18-48 years; 84.6% women), including 53 with current major depressive disorder and 58 healthy controls. Prior to functional MRI scanning, participants received either 50 mg of amisulpride, a low-dose dopamine D2/D3 antagonist that enhances dopaminergic signalling, or placebo in a double-blind, randomized design. Approximately 1 h later, coinciding with peak plasma concentration, participants completed a reward task in the scanner. Individualized cortical parcellations were derived from functional MRI data, followed by edge-centric connectomes. Specifically, functional connections (edges) were clustered into communities, allowing brain regions to participate in multiple networks. Entropy and functional diversity were computed to quantify network overlap within canonical large-scale brain systems. Three-way mixed ANOVA (diagnosis, drug, canonical brain system) tested the effects of major depressive disorder and dopamine on network overlap. Elastic net regression was applied to predict depression severity and anhedonia from network overlap measures. Individuals with major depressive disorder exhibited greater functional diversity, indicating reduced similarity in connectivity profiles among regions assigned to the same brain system. Across all participants, dopamine tended to reduce brain entropy, providing preliminary evidence for a less overlapping network organization. Measures of network overlap predicted anhedonia and depression severity, with limbic and visual networks contributing most strongly. Collectively, these findings indicate that individual differences in brain network overlap track depressive symptomatology and are sensitive to dopaminergic modulation. Ultimately, these measures may serve as markers for monitoring disease progression and predicting clinical outcomes.

title: The Genetic Architecture of Essential Tremor.
journal: Tremor and other hyperkinetic movements (New York, N.Y.)
abstract: Essential tremor (ET) is the most common adult movement disorder with a reported global prevalence of 0.32%-0.9%, rising to 4.6-6.3% in those >65 years [12345]. Autosomal dominant patterns of inheritance have been reported in some multiplex ET families; genetic studies continue to yield heterogenous results [67]. Despite numerous reported genes and loci, replication has been inconsistent and the relative strength of genetic findings varies considerably [89]. To provide a comprehensive overview of advances in ET genetics over the last decade, synthesising evidence across contemporary genetic approaches and identifying key gaps and priorities for future research. PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science were searched for human genetic studies of ET published between 2015 and 2025. Eligible studies included candidate-gene, genome-wide association, family-based sequencing and other genomic approaches. Following screening and hand-searching of reference lists, 33 studies were included. Genetic findings were highly heterogeneous. Evidence included common susceptibility loci with small effects, rare family-specific variants, repeat expansions and candidate-gene associations, but independent replication was limited. Most studies also used diagnostic criteria predating the 2018 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society (IPMDS) tremor classification. Current evidence supports a complex and heterogeneous genetic architecture for ET rather than a single genetic model. Larger ancestry-diverse cohorts, consistent longitudinal phenotyping, independent replication and integration of genomic findings with functional and molecular approaches are required to establish biologically and clinically relevant genetic determinants.

title: Collapse of local circuit integrated information Φ during NREM sleep.
abstract: Clarifying the mechanisms underlying the emergence of consciousness remains a fundamental challenge in modern neuroscience. Integrated Information Theory (IIT) provides a mathematical framework derived from the phenomenological properties of consciousness as its axioms. IIT proposes that consciousness is identical to a system's intrinsic cause-effect information structure, quantified by integrated information Φ. While IIT predicts that the Φ of a neuronal system should decrease during the loss of consciousness, this hypothesis has remained untested at the neural circuit level. The present study provides empirical support for this IIT prediction. It was found that Φ within local circuits decreases during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep compared to wakefulness (and REM sleep in the frontal cortex), regardless of cortical laminar structure. The reduction in Φ was particularly pronounced during OFF-periods, when neural activity is collectively suppressed. These results align with IIT's framework, suggesting that the loss of consciousness corresponds to a collapse of integrated information within local circuits. The findings provide empirical support for IIT as a mathematical theory aiming to explain conscious experiences.

title: Neuroimmune-endocrine interactions in perinatal asphyxia: from brain injury to neuroprotection.
abstract: Perinatal asphyxia (PA) remains a major cause of neonatal mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental disability worldwide. Although hypoxic-ischemic brain injury has traditionally been attributed to oxygen deprivation, excitotoxicity, and oxidative stress, accumulating evidence indicates that neurological outcomes are determined by complex interactions among metabolic, mitochondrial, neuroimmune, and neuroendocrine mechanisms. Following hypoxic-ischemic injury, primary energy failure rapidly triggers excitotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, calcium dysregulation, and oxidative damage, leading to activation of microglia and astrocytes, release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, disruption of blood-brain barrier integrity, and recruitment of peripheral immune cells. These events contribute to the development of secondary energy failure and persistent neuroinflammation. Simultaneously, activation of hypoxia-responsive pathways, including hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1), heat shock protein 70 (HSP70), glutathione-dependent antioxidant defenses, and neuroendocrine stress responses involving the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, promote endogenous adaptation and neuroprotection. Nitric oxide signaling further links mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative and nitrosative stress, inflammatory activation, and neuronal injury. Together, these mechanisms form an integrated neuroimmune-endocrine network that influences both injury progression and tissue repair. In this review, we propose Brain Energy Failure as a unifying conceptual framework linking mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative and nitrosative stress, neuroinflammation, endocrine adaptation, and endogenous neuroprotective responses following perinatal hypoxia. We further discuss the role of biomarkers associated with neuro-immuno-endocrine dysfunction, including inflammatory mediators, oxidative stress markers, endocrine factors, and indicators of neuronal and glial injury. Recent evidence has highlighted the therapeutic potential of multimodal neuroprotective approaches, including endogenous lipid mediators such as palmitoylethanolamide (PEA), which exert anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and mitoprotective effects. We also review current and emerging neuroprotective strategies targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling, and bioenergetic instability, and discuss their translational implications. Understanding the interactions among these interconnected pathways may facilitate biomarker-guided diagnosis, personalized neuroprotection, and the development of more effective therapies aimed at improving long-term neurological outcomes following perinatal asphyxia.

title: The Effect of Early-Onset Spasticity on Independent Outdoor Ambulation After Motor-Incomplete (AIS D) Traumatic Spinal Cord Injury: A Retrospective Longitudinal Cohort Study.
journal: Topics in spinal cord injury rehabilitation
abstract: To determine whether early-onset spasticity during acute care is associated with reduced odds of independent outdoor ambulation after motor-incomplete (AIS D) traumatic spinal cord injury (TSCI) and to explore whether initiation of oral baclofen during acute care influenced this association. This retrospective longitudinal cohort study was conducted at a single level I trauma center specialized in acute SCI care. A cohort of 137 adults with AIS D TSCI admitted between July 2013 and January 2025 was enrolled and followed for at least 6 months after injury. Early-onset spasticity during acute hospitalization was defined as increased muscle tone (Modified Ashworth Scale ≥1), observed spasms/clonus, or patient-reported spasms/clonus. Independent outdoor ambulation at follow-up was defined as a Spinal Cord Independence Measure (SCIM III) item 14 score ≥7. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between early-onset spasticity and independent outdoor ambulation while adjusting for age, Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI ≥3 vs. 0-2), and baseline total motor score (≥83 vs. <83). Sensitivity analyses examined length of stay and baclofen use. Early-onset spasticity occurred in 46/137 participants (33.6%), and 99/137 (72.3%) achieved independent outdoor ambulation at follow-up. In multivariable analysis, early-onset spasticity (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.09-0.59, P = .01) and CCI ≥3 (OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.06-0.79, P = .02) were independently associated with lower odds of independent outdoor ambulation. Findings remained consistent in sensitivity analyses adjusting for length of stay, inpatient rehabilitation discharge, and baclofen use. Early-onset spasticity during acute care is independently associated with reduced odds of recovering independent outdoor ambulation after AIS D TSCI. Assessment of early spasticity may provide clinically relevant prognostic information.

title: Circadian Disruption and Chrono-rehabilitation After Spinal Cord Injury.
journal: Topics in spinal cord injury rehabilitation
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) disrupts circadian biology through multiple mechanisms, including dysregulation of core clock genes, inversion of melatonin secretion rhythms, blunted thermoregulatory oscillations, and loss of autonomic pathways that relay timing signals from the suprachiasmatic nucleus to peripheral tissues. These disruptions affect the processes on which rehabilitation depends, that is, neuroplasticity, motor learning consolidation, inflammatory modulation, and tissue repair. Despite this, circadian assessment and intervention remain absent from standard SCI rehabilitation protocols. It can be argued that restoring temporal organization is not ancillary to SCI rehabilitation but is a prerequisite for optimizing functional recovery. However, the evidence underpinning many of the proposed interventions is largely derived from non-SCI populations or preclinical models, and direct clinical trial data in SCI rehabilitation remain limited. Herein, the authors propose a chronobiological framework for SCI rehabilitation that includes systematic sleep-wake assessment using actigraphy and validated questionnaires, timed bright light therapy, individually dosed melatonin supplementation, and scheduling of intensive therapy sessions during patients' peak neurocognitive and motor performance windows. The integration of circadian medicine into SCI rehabilitation requires a shift in perspective; patients are not temporally neutral and their recovery potential is modulated by circadian function.

title: Computational and Experimental Studies of PSMA-Targeted Conjugates Designed for Subcellular Delivery of Theranostic Radiometals to Prostate Cancer Cells.
abstract: Background: The membrane receptor prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is a validated target for theranostic radioconjugates in the treatment and imaging of prostate cancer (PCa). Radioconjugates targeted at PSMA rely mostly on the peptidomimetic glutamate-urea-lysine (Glu-urea-Lys) binding motif to facilitate tumor accumulation. The combination of this binding motif with subcellular targeting moieties, such as acridine orange (AO) and triphenylphosphonium (TPP) derivatives, for nuclear and mitochondrial delivery, respectively, might open the way to innovative dual-target approaches. This study integrated molecular docking, long-timescale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and in vitro PSMA inhibition assays to assess whether the incorporation of AO or TPP disrupts the canonical PSMA binding in DOTA-based conjugates containing the Glu-urea-Lys binding motif designed by our group. Results: Docking analyses indicated that our PSMA-targeted conjugates carrying AO or TPP moieties adopt poses analogous to those of PSMA's natural substrate N-acetyl-aspartyl-glutamate (NAAG) and of the reference conjugate natIn-PSMA-617, preserving crucial interactions within the arginine-rich S1 pocket and within the glutamate-sensing S1' pocket. In contrast, their congeners lacking the Glu-urea-Lys binding motif exhibited surface-associated binding but failed to engage stably within the active site of PSMA. MD simulations confirmed the structural stability of the PSMA-conjugate complexes. In vitro inhibition assays supported these observations: the non-PSMA-targeted natIn-AO and natIn-TPP displayed negligible inhibitory activity against PSMA (with noncalculable IC50 values), whereas the dual-target conjugates displayed potency in the submicromolar range. Conclusion: Collectively, our results show that the dual-target conjugates recognize the PSMA protein, with subcellular targeting motifs influencing peripheral dynamics, but not core binding. This framework supports the rational design of multifunctional PSMA-directed radioconjugates for improved subcellular delivery of theranostic radionuclides toward alternative In PCa imaging and management.

title: Viroimmunotherapy in 9p21.3-deleted gliomas.
abstract: One of the most frequent genetic alterations in high-grade gliomas is the homozygous deletion of the 9p21.3 chromosomal region, affecting 20%-50% of tumors. The 9p21.3 locus encodes key tumor suppressor genes (CDKN2A and CDKN2B), MTAP, and a cluster of type I interferon (IFN) genes. The loss of CDKN2A and CDKN2B deregulates the Rb and p53 pathways, driving uncontrolled proliferation and creating a replication-permissive state that oncolytic viruses can exploit. The simultaneous deletion of MTAP and type I IFN genes impairs innate immune surveillance, thereby enhancing viral replication but limiting the host's capacity for adaptive immune priming. Hence, current evidence suggests that 9p21.3 deletions eliminate a proliferative block and promote immune evasion, contributing to tumorigenesis. Despite the high frequency of 9p21.3 loss in malignant gliomas, the extent to which this deletion affects the therapeutic efficacy of oncolytic viruses remains unclear. In this review, we discuss the potential of using 9p21.3 status as a biomarker of therapeutic response, the challenges of modeling 9p21.3 loss in preclinical glioma models, and future strategies to exploit oncolytic viral permissiveness while stimulating antitumor immunity in patients with high-grade gliomas and 9p21.3 loss.

title: Integrating Evidence Generation and Commercialization in Digital Medicine: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Digital medicine requires evaluation of clinical effects, delivery conditions, and the resources needed for use in practice. This narrative review examines how evidence requirements differ across clinical evaluation, regulatory authorization, purchasing, implementation, and postmarket assessment, using digital therapeutics as the principal illustrative application. Targeted searches of public literature and regulatory sources were supplemented with searches for additional studies of digital care delivery, economic outcomes, and implementation. Sources were selected for relevance to a defined evidence question; no systematic study enumeration or quantitative pooling was undertaken. Published examples include aphasia rehabilitation, migraine prevention, major depressive disorder, schizophrenia, digital pain care, insomnia-related primary care costs, and implementation of substance use disorder treatment. The synthesis distinguishes randomized treatment effects from exploratory analyses, engagement from clinical benefit, regulatory status from purchasing evidence, and observed resource use from modeled economic consequences. The examples show why comparator choice, analysis population, human support, software version, and follow-up duration matter when translating findings to a different setting. A nonsignificant primary analysis remains distinct from a favorable supportive analysis, and low uptake in routine care identifies an implementation problem without independently resolving efficacy. Original tables and conceptual figures organize these distinctions using established evidence-planning, implementation, economic, and measurement frameworks. The review does not rank products or establish that an evidence strategy causes commercial success. Evidence generation can inform commercialization when claims remain traceable to the intervention studied, the comparison performed, and the uncertainty that remains for the intended decision maker.

title: Development and In Vitro Evaluation of Kaempferol-Loaded Liposomes in LN-229 Glioblastoma Cells: Potency, Selectivity, and Modulation of ROS-Dependent Cytotoxicity.
abstract: Glioblastoma multiforme has a median survival of 12-15 months despite multimodal treatment, due to blood-brain barrier impermeability limiting CNS drug bioavailability. Liposomal nanoformulations circumvent this barrier while offering tunable surface chemistry and amphiphilic drug-loading capacity. Here, we report encapsulation of kaempferol, a dietary flavonoid, within phosphatidylcholine-cholesterol liposomes (Lip-KPF) and evaluate cytotoxic activity against LN-229 glioblastoma cells relative to free kaempferol (KPF) and puromycin aminonucleoside (Puro-A). LCMS confirmed 56% encapsulation efficiency; dynamic light scattering yielded a zeta potential of -15.32 ± 0.83 mV, mean particle size of 200.44 ± 12.22 nm, and PDI of 0.29 ± 0.06, with 31P NMR confirming a multilamellar structure. Lip-KPF potency against LN-229 cells increased progressively across 24-72 h, peaking at 72 h (19.880 μM) with significantly lower IC50 values than free KPF (p < 0.001), while maintaining lower astrocyte toxicity. Selectivity indices for Lip-KPF exceeded 1 at every time point, widening over time. Cell death was confirmed by TUNEL assay and phase-contrast microscopy. RT-qPCR revealed concurrent BAX and TP53 upregulation alongside CASP3/CASP7 suppression in both groups, with no significant difference between KPF and Lip-KPF; ELISA corroborated CASP3 suppression, consistent with a possible caspase-independent death mechanism. In a preliminary antioxidant rescue assay, pretreatment did not significantly alter KPF-induced cytotoxicity but significantly increased it in Lip-KPF-treated cells, indicating a cytotoxic mechanism independent of the ROS pathway contributing to free KPF's activity. These findings support Lip-KPF as a candidate for continued preclinical investigation in LN-229 glioblastoma cells.

title: A culturally and linguistically tailored web-based decision aid for dementia care decision-making among Chinese American family caregivers: feasibility and preliminary effects.
abstract: Chinese American family caregivers face cultural and logistical barriers to accessing dementia care services. This study evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, usability, and preliminary signals of benefit of a culturally and linguistically tailored, web-based decision aid for dementia care decision-making. This study used a two-phase design comprising usability and acceptability testing followed by a single-arm pre-post evaluation to assess the feasibility, acceptability, and usability of the decision aid among Chinese American family caregivers (N = 74) who had provided care to a family member with dementia or dementia-related symptoms and to report preliminary outcomes on changes in dementia care knowledge and decisional conflict. The decision aid demonstrated high acceptability and usability. All participants rated the length and informational content as appropriate, and the tool was perceived as easy to use, informative, and helpful for decision-making. Consistent with predefined progression criteria, significant improvements were observed in dementia care knowledge, particularly in home and long-term care. Decisional conflict was significantly reduced, reflecting greater understanding of care options, clearer perceptions of benefits and risks, and increased confidence in decision-making. Decision-related outcomes improved following exposure, indicating greater clarity and confidence in decision-making. Findings suggest that this culturally and linguistically tailored decision aid met early-phase progression criteria for acceptability, usability, and improvement in proximal outcomes, supporting its advancement to the next phase of testing. Future research should evaluate behavioral and longer-term outcomes, all of which will be important for subsequent controlled trials.

title: Psychometric Validation of the Arabic Version of the Anxiety Sensitivity Index-3 (ASI-3) in a Saudi University Sample.
abstract: To translate the Anxiety Sensitivity Index-3 (ASI-3) into Arabic, culturally adapt it to an Arabic context, and evaluate its psychometric properties in a Saudi university sample. A cross-sectional psychometric validation study was conducted among 500 Saudi university students (mean age = 22.7 ± 5.77 years; 60% female). The ASI-3 was translated and culturally adapted according to the cross-cultural adaptation guidelines proposed by Beaton et al. Subsequently, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) were conducted to evaluate the tool's factorial validity. Criterion-related validity was assessed via the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS-12) and the Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale (GAD-7). Additionally, known-groups validity, predictive validity, and internal consistency reliability were evaluated. The PCA supported the original three-factor structure of the ASI-3 (physical, cognitive, and social concerns), thereby explaining 81.04% of the total variance, with factor loadings ranging from 0.85 to 0.90. Furthermore, CFA supported the proposed measurement model with favorable fit indices. The Arabic ASI-3 demonstrated satisfactory criterion-related validity, showing significant positive correlations with the IUS-12 and GAD-7 (r = 0.63-0.75, p < 0.01), which remained significant after controlling for age and gender. Additionally, known-groups analyses demonstrated large effect sizes (Cohen's d = 1.50-2.30), while regression analyses indicated that ASI-3 scores explained 54.6% of the variance in intolerance of uncertainty and 56.9% of the variance in generalized anxiety. Additionally, the instrument demonstrated high internal consistency, with Cronbach's alpha coefficients ranging from 0.85 to 0.95. Based on its evaluation in a Saudi university sample, the Arabic ASI-3 demonstrated satisfactory psychometric properties. Overall, the findings support its use as a reliable measure of anxiety sensitivity in research settings, thereby providing a robust foundation for its future validation in more diverse community and clinical populations in Saudi Arabia.

title: Pediatric Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis: Insights into Risk Profiles, Imaging Features, and Management Outcomes from a Single-Center Cohort.
abstract: To characterize the clinical presentation, risk factors, neuroimaging findings, management strategies, and outcomes of pediatric cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST). We retrospectively reviewed electronic medical records of pediatric patients with imaging-confirmed CVST at a tertiary care center in Jeddah, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Demographics, clinical features, risk factors, laboratory and imaging findings, management, and outcomes were analyzed. Descriptive statistics, bivariate analyses, and linear regression were performed. Seventeen patients were included (mean age 4.6 years, 64% male). Altered level of consciousness (58%), seizures (41%), and headache (35%) were the most common presentations. Infection was the predominant risk factor (71%), including sepsis (35%), meningitis (29%), otitis media (18%), and mastoiditis (18%). Extensive or multiple sinus thrombosis occurred in 58% of patients; isolated right transverse sinus thrombosis was most frequent (24%). Anticoagulation was administered to 88% of patients (primarily low-molecular-weight heparin) with no major bleeding complications. Follow-up imaging (35% of patients) showed complete recanalization in 4 and persistent thrombosis in 2. One patient died (5.9% mortality). Infection was significantly associated with altered consciousness (OR 18.0, p = 0.02). Age did not predict extent of sinus involvement (p = 0.44). Pediatric CVST in this cohort is strongly linked to infection, which frequently presents with altered mental status. Anticoagulation appears safe and well tolerated. Larger prospective studies are needed to standardize treatment protocols and assess long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.

title: Impact of Digital Addiction in Adolescents: Cognitive Deficits, Emotional Dysregulation, and Neurophysiological Alterations - A Systematic Review.
abstract: To synthesize evidence on the cognitive and neural impacts of digital addiction in adolescents. Ten studies published between 2010 and 2024 were reviewed using databases such as PubMed, Scopus, and PsycINFO. Data were extracted for quantitative synthesis, and meta-analysis was performed where possible. Meta-analysis revealed a pooled effect size of 0.71 (95% CI: 0.60-0.82). Findings include a 25% reduction in sustained attention, a 30% decline in memory linked to hippocampal activity, and up to 15% reductions in grey matter volume in critical brain regions. Emotional regulation challenges, including mood instability, correlated with heightened reward system activity. The findings highlight the urgent need for targeted interventions to mitigate the adverse effects of digital addiction on adolescent brain development, ensuring balanced cognitive and emotional growth.

title: Organelle distribution and protein translation defects in radial glia cells with mutations in Eml1.
abstract: Cerebral cortical development is a finely regulated process, depending on key neuronal progenitors, giving rise to neurons that migrate to superficial regions in the brain. Disruptions can cause severe cortical malformations, associated with intellectual disability and epilepsy. Mutations in EML1/Eml1, a microtubule-associated protein, lead to subcortical heterotopia in humans and mice. In mutant mouse brains, ectopic apical radial glia (aRG) progenitors were found outside the proliferative ventricular zone. The role of Eml1 in these cells remains unclear. Using proteomics and imaging approaches, we reveal that Eml1 regulates mitochondrial trafficking within aRG in vivo and influences mitochondrial and polysome distribution. Furthermore, Eml1 associates with translational machinery, and an overall downregulation of translation is observed in the Eml1 mutant aRG translatome. Paradoxically, an upregulation of translation-related mRNAs is also observed. These findings indicate that Eml1 regulates fundamental cellular mechanisms, including translation, crucial for aRG function and brain architecture.

title: When one letter matters: Distinguishing VGF from VEGF in biomedical research.
abstract: Scientific communication relies heavily on abbreviations to simplify complex terminology. When abbreviations are similar yet represent biologically distinct molecules; however, confusion can arise with consequences for literature interpretation, data retrieval, and scientific communication. One example is the recurring visual similarity between vascular growth factor (VGF; or proVGF), a neuroprotein precursor implicated in neuronal development, synaptic plasticity, metabolism, and neuropsychiatric disease, and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), a key regulator of angiogenesis and vascular function. Although these proteins belong to entirely different biological systems, their near-identical abbreviations create a structural risk of misreading among students, researchers, reviewers, and clinicians, a risk that may grow as literature search and screening increasingly rely on automated and AI-based tools. Here, we discuss the origins of this naming overlap, contrast the distinct biological roles of VGF and VEGF, and propose practical recommendations to reduce ambiguity in scientific communication.

title: PCSK9 inhibitors and atherosclerotic plaque regression and stabilisation across major arterial beds: a systematic review with narrative synthesis.
abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors lower low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) by about 50-60% beyond statin therapy and reduce major adverse cardiovascular events. Whether these agents change atherosclerotic plaque burden and composition, and whether such changes are consistent across arterial beds, has been addressed in individual imaging trials but not in a synthesis restricted to traceable, design-appropriate contrasts. MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science, Scopus and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception through 31 May 2025. Two designs were eligible and were analysed separately: parallel-group randomised trials with a concurrent comparator, contributing the between-group difference in change from baseline, and single-arm or historical-control cohorts, contributing descriptive within-subject changes only. Studies without a traceable publication, or without a registry record matching the tabulated results, were excluded. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohorts. Findings were synthesised narratively, structured by design, arterial bed and imaging endpoint; no meta-analysis was performed. The protocol is registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261379883). The primary evidence set comprised the citable parallel-group imaging trials GLAGOV, PACMAN-AMI, HUYGENS, ODYSSEY J-IVUS, ALTAIR and ANITSCHKOW. ARCHITECT and YELLOW III were retained as single-arm descriptive studies and were not pooled. In GLAGOV, evolocumab changed percent atheroma volume by -0.95% versus +0.05% with placebo (between-group difference -1.00%). In PACMAN-AMI, alirocumab changed percent atheroma volume by -2.13% versus -0.92% (between-group -1.21%), minimum fibrous-cap thickness by +62.7 versus +33.2 μm (between-group +29.5 μm), and maxLCBI4mm by -79.4 versus -37.6 units (between-group -41.8). In HUYGENS, minimum fibrous-cap thickness increased by +42.7 versus +21.5 μm (between-group +21.2 μm) and percent atheroma volume changed by -2.29% versus -0.61% (P = 0.009). ODYSSEY J-IVUS did not show a significant between-group difference in normalised total atheroma volume (-4.8% versus -3.1%; P = 0.23) or percent atheroma volume (-1.4% versus -1.3%; nominal P = 0.79). ANITSCHKOW did not meet its primary carotid 18F-FDG endpoint. EVOCAR-1 did not show a significant between-group reduction in lipid-rich necrotic-core volume. No pooled estimate is reported. PCSK9 inhibitors are associated with favourable changes in selected imaging surrogates of atherosclerotic plaque burden and composition, predominantly in coronary imaging studies of parallel-group trials. These changes are consistent with, but do not independently establish, a biological mechanism for the cardiovascular and cerebrovascular event reductions observed in outcome trials.

title: Transformer-based EEG source imaging localizes pathological high-frequency oscillations in focal epilepsy.
abstract: High-frequency oscillations are specific biomarkers of the epileptogenic zone, yet their non-invasive localization from scalp EEG remains challenging due to their brief duration, low amplitude and poor signal-to-noise ratio. Here, we introduce a transformer-based high-frequency oscillation deep source-imaging framework (TH-DeepSIF) trained on biologically realistic neural mass model simulations for non-invasive high-frequency oscillation source imaging. The model was evaluated in simulated single- and dual-source scenarios, where it recovered both the spatial location and temporal dynamics of high-frequency oscillation generators under increasing spatiotemporal complexity. We further validated TH-DeepSIF in 20 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy by comparing reconstructed high-frequency oscillation sources with surgical resection regions. TH-DeepSIF achieved accurate localization and waveform reconstruction in simulations, demonstrating low localization error and strong temporal correspondence with ground truth. In clinical data, pathological high-frequency oscillations (spike ripples) showed strong agreement with resection regions, with a median localization error of 10.9 mm and specificity of 0.883. In a subset of six patients with intracranial EEG, pathological high-frequency oscillation source estimates were spatially close to the seizure onset zone (median localization error: 2.41 mm). Compared with all detected high-frequency oscillations, imaging based on pathological high-frequency oscillations yielded significantly improved spatial correspondence and performance across multiple metrics. Reconstructed source activity was also temporally aligned with both scalp high-frequency oscillation bursts and associated spike deflections. These results demonstrate that TH-DeepSIF provides a data-driven framework for non-invasive high-frequency oscillation source imaging with improved anatomical specificity and support the use of pathological high-frequency oscillations as informative biomarkers for epileptogenic zone localization.

title: Beyond emotional hunger: exploring the microbiota-gut-brain axis as a proposed mechanistic framework for emotional eating.
