abstract: Emotional eating (EE), characterized by food intake in response to affective states rather than physiological hunger, has traditionally been conceptualized through psychological models of stress, emotion dysregulation, and reward-driven behaviour. These frameworks, however, do not fully explain interindividual differences in vulnerability or the persistence of maladaptive eating patterns. This narrative review critically examines the microbiota-gut-brain axis as a potential mechanistic framework linking psychological, neurobiological, and nutritional determinants of emotional eating. Evidence from psychology, neuroscience, microbiology, and nutritional psychiatry is integrated to evaluate the roles of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation, reward processing, neurotransmitter metabolism, immune signaling, appetite-related hormones, and microbial metabolites. Emerging findings suggest that gut microbial composition and function may influence mood, stress responsivity, food craving, and eating behaviour through neural, endocrine, immune, and metabolic pathways. Most of this evidence, however, derives from animal models, mechanistic in vitro work, or human studies of stress, depression, obesity and general appetite regulation; comparatively few studies have measured emotional eating itself as an outcome, and the pathways described should therefore be read as candidate rather than established mechanisms. Dietary patterns may further modify these interactions by shaping microbial diversity, inflammatory tone, and metabolite production. Although current evidence is consistent with a plausible bidirectional relationship between gut-brain signaling and emotional eating, direct causal evidence in humans remains limited and the direction of the association is unresolved. EE should therefore be understood as a multidimensional biopsychological phenomenon. Future longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to clarify causal pathways and evaluate integrated psychological, nutritional, and microbiome-targeted strategies for personalized prevention and management in diverse clinical populations.

title: The infinity object: neurophenomenology and psychoanalytic corollaries of near-death experiences.
abstract: As technological advances have occurred in medicine, including improvements in rates of resuscitation, descriptions of near-death experiences (NDEs) have increased significantly. However, NDEs have been present within religious, literary, and biographical texts for centuries. The phenomenology of NDEs encompasses an inward journey wherein review of one's life, seeing the dead, and an encounter with a spiritually powerful "being of light" may be reported. The subjective transformations that take place in survivors, as well as the insights generated from NDEs, can be linked with dimensions of the depressive position and Bion's concept of O. The neurophenomenology of NDEs will be discussed, focusing primarily on neurotransmitter systems. Parallels and contrasts from psychedelic literature will also be explored. Drawing from these various dimensions, the concept of the infinity object will be outlined.

title: Comprehensive Fertility Management in Men with Spinal Cord Injury from Optimization to Assisted Reproduction: A Systematic Review.
journal: Topics in spinal cord injury rehabilitation
abstract: To evaluate fertility preservation (FP) procedures, fertility optimization strategies, and reproductive management approaches in adult men with spinal cord injury (SCI). A systematic review of the literature published from January 1990 to July 2025 was conducted following the PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251001147). The review included studies on FP techniques and broader fertility management strategies evaluating sperm retrieval rates, semen quality, and pregnancy and live birth rates, as well as factors influencing infertility risk, including sperm parameters, cryopreservation outcomes, and ejaculation rates. The search identified 434 articles, 67 of which were included. A sequential FP algorithm including masturbation, penile vibratory stimulation (PVS), electroejaculation (EEJ), and surgical methods allowed retrieval of sperm in 75% to 86% of men with SCI. The pregnancy rate ranged between 33.9% and 73.7%, and the live birth rate was 41%. Bladder management by intermittent self-catheterization (ISC) consistently reduced infection rates and improved sperm motility. Leukocytospermia was not directly linked to impaired sperm parameters, although it may reflect inflammation or oxidative stress. Cytokine-neutralizing strategies and pharmacological agents, such as probenecid, displayed promising but preliminary results requiring confirmation in large prospective studies. Fertility management in men with SCI relies on a combination of sperm retrieval techniques, assisted reproductive technologies, and optimization of modifiable infertility-related factors. These approaches should be tailored to the patient's needs and SCI characteristics. Among strategies to reduce infertility risk, ISC appears to be associated with improved outcomes. A multidisciplinary approach is essential for individualized, evidence-based care.

title: Dance-based exercise for healthy brain aging in older adults: integrating neuroplasticity, cognitive reserve, physical fitness, social engagement, and mental well-being.
abstract: Population aging brings rising difficulties associated with cognitive deterioration, diminished physical capabilities, social isolation, and increased susceptibility to mental health problems. Finding accessible, multidomain approaches to promote healthy brain aging has become a major priority. Dance-based exercise is a distinctive form of physical activity that combines aerobic movement, motor coordination, cognitive involvement, social interaction, and emotional expression. Previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses have largely quantified isolated physical or cognitive outcomes following dance interventions. However, an accurate understanding of healthy brain aging requires synthesizing how these separate domains interact. This narrative review adds to the current literature by providing an integrated conceptual framework that connects the neurobiological, physical, and psychosocial dimensions of dance-based exercise. Rather than pooling isolated effect sizes, we examine theoretical mechanisms (e.g., task-specific neuroplasticity and cognitive reserve) that plausibly link multidomain elements of dance to brain aging; these mechanisms are primarily hypothesis-generating in the context of existing dance trials. This narrative review examines the potential mechanisms by which dance-based exercise may support healthy brain aging in older adults, emphasizing neuroplasticity, cognitive reserve, physical fitness, social participation, and psychological well-being. The evidence available indicates that dance-based interventions may be linked to gains in cognitive functioning, especially executive abilities and attention, along with improvements in balance, mobility, and functional performance. In addition, the social and enjoyable character of dance may help foster better psychological outcomes and emotional well-being, although current evidence specifically concerning loneliness remains mixed. However, differences across study designs, intervention protocols, participant characteristics, and outcome measures constrain the ability to draw definitive conclusions about causality and the most effective intervention parameters. New evidence suggests that dance-based exercise may offer a promising multidomain strategy for strengthening resilience and supporting brain health throughout aging. Further rigorously designed longitudinal studies and randomized controlled trials are required to elucidate the underlying mechanisms, determine which populations are most responsive, and develop evidence-based guidance for incorporating dance-based interventions into healthy aging and geriatric mental health approaches.

title: From gut education to central infiltration: microbiota-driven immune trafficking along the gut-brain axis.
abstract: The classical paradigm of central nervous system (CNS) immune privilege has evolved toward recognizing a dynamic, multi-organ neuroimmune axis. In recent years, the gastrointestinal tract has been widely recognized as a major immune reservoir, where rather than functioning as a localized physical barrier, the gastrointestinal mucosa acts as a vital educational center that instructs systemic immune responses. Within the gut-associated lymphoid tissue, dietary inputs, microbial metabolites, and commensal colonization imprint intestinal adaptive and innate immune cells with distinct functional phenotypes and migratory signatures. Through coordinated molecular mechanisms, these gut-educated immune cells egress from the mucosa to reach distant sites, with the CNS representing a critical destination. In experimental models, under homeostatic conditions, gut-derived signals direct the physiological seeding of central border zones and parenchyma, where specialized populations maintain baseline tissue surveillance, reinforce barrier integrity, and calibrate neurodevelopmental behaviors. Conversely, pathobiont expansion, loss of short-chain fatty acid-producing commensals, and mucosal barrier disruption predominantly promote pathogenic gut priming, transforming gut-resident cells into autoreactive or pro-inflammatory effectors that breach central neurovascular borders. Once inside the CNS, these gut immune cells can contribute to neurodegeneration, ischemic injury, and neuroinflammatory pathology. However, this migration is not always destructive; specific gut-educated populations are simultaneously deployed to central boundaries to execute anti-inflammatory and counter-regulatory protection. By tracing this microbiota-driven intestinal priming to central infiltration, we highlight shared homing mechanisms identified mainly in preclinical models (mouse models, germ-free and photoconvertible animals), while outlining translational challenges in establishing their role in human neuroinflammatory pathology.

title: Temporal evolution acquisition based arterial spin labeling (TEA-ASL) for accurate estimation of apparent T2 of perfusion signal in brain.
abstract: Accurate quantification of apparent transverse relaxation (T2) in the brain can be useful for non-invasive assessment of blood oxygenation and blood-brain barrier (BBB) function. While arterial spin labeling (ASL) combined with multi-echo readouts offers a contrast-agent-free approach to map apparent T2, in vivo applications remain challenging due to rapid signal decay and low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at longer echo times (TEs), likely leading to overestimation of T2 values. We propose a novel temporal evolution acquisition based ASL (TEA-ASL) sequence incorporating an optimized variable refocusing flip angle (RFA) train to preserve signal across all TEs. Data were acquired on a 5T MRI system combining a pseudo-continuous ASL (pCASL) with the proposed TEA readout with 12 echo times (32-384 ms). The variable RFA scheme significantly improved signal stability across the echo train compared to conventional acquisition with constant RFAs. Accuracy and clinical feasibility of the proposed method was validated by simulations, phantom scans, in-vivo test/retest experiments and in a patient with middle cerebral artery stenosis. The proposed TEA-ASL technique provides robust apparent T2 mapping in the brain at ultra-high field, offering a promising tool for probing oxygenation-related haemodynamics and BBB-associated pathophysiology.

title: Plant Dehydrin-Derived, Lysine-Rich Peptides Show Both Antifungal Activity and Blood-Brain Barrier Penetration.
abstract: The plant-based, dehydrin-derived peptides represent an underexplored source of antifungal agents. In this study, we investigated the antifungal activity, cellular association, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability of a lysine-rich peptide (ERD-A) derived from the Arabidopsis thaliana dehydrin ERD14, as well as its rationally designed sequence variants. The amino acid substitutions were engineered to modulate charge, aromatic residue content, and conformational flexibility. Antifungal activity was assessed against clinically relevant yeasts, including Candida albicans, Candidozyma auris, and Cryptococcus neoformans. The parental ERD-A peptide exhibited moderate activity against C. albicans and C. neoformans, while most variants showed species-dependent changes in potency. Increased cationicity or introduction of tryptophan residues enhanced activity against C. neoformans, with several variants displaying 4-fold lower MIC values than the parental peptide. In contrast, C. auris showed limited susceptibility to all tested variants. Fluorescence microscopy and flow cytometry demonstrated strong, time-dependent cell association of carboxyfluorescein-labeled ERD-A in C. albicans, reaching ∼98 to 99% positive cells after 16 h. BBB permeability was evaluated using an in vitro model of cocultured human brain endothelial cells with pericytes. All ERD-A-derived peptides exhibited higher permeability than that of the reference BBB-penetrating peptide opiorphin. The parental peptide showed high permeability, and selected variants retained or slightly improved this property. All these results demonstrate that ERD-A constitutes a tunable antifungal scaffold in which targeted sequence modifications modulate antifungal activity while preserving cell-penetrating and BBB-crossing properties. These features highlight ERD-A-derived peptides as candidates for multifunctional antifungal agents, particularly for central nervous system infections.

title: Cell membrane-coated nanoparticles for brain diseases: Processing, membrane-derived functions and translational challenges.
abstract: Brain diseases such as glioblastoma (GBM), Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and ischemic stroke remain difficult to treat in part because the blood-brain barrier (BBB) restricts and spatially controls the entry of many therapeutic agents. Cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (CNPs) integrate cell-derived membrane shells with nanoparticle cores made of polymeric, lipid-based, or inorganic materials, offering promising biomimetic platforms for brain drug delivery. This review summarizes CNP fabrication and characterization methods and discusses how molecules associated with specific membrane sources and disease-specific delivery barriers inform platform design. Major membrane sources, including red blood cells, immune cells, stem cells, cancer cells, and platelets, are compared in terms of their relevant surface molecules, recognition mechanisms, potential delivery functions, and limitations. We further discuss how preparation and functionalization affect coating integrity, membrane-protein accessibility, and payload retention, and outline key challenges in reproducible manufacturing, biosafety, and clinical translation. This review provides a framework for evaluating CNP design and for assessing the evidence supporting brain-targeted delivery.

title: Active L2 immersion is associated with glymphatic-related MRI markers in healthy young adults: A cross-sectional multimodal study.
abstract: The brain's glymphatic system plays a vital role in maintaining neural health. However, little is known about whether second language (L2) immersion is associated with glymphatic function. 50 high-proficiency L2 English speakers (mean age: 32.6 years; 78% female) underwent multimodal MRI. Three glymphatic-related markers were derived: BOLD-CSF coupling strength (fMRI), choroid plexus (ChP) ratio (structural MRI), and DTI-ALPS index (diffusion MRI). We examined their associations with L2 immersion duration and age of acquisition (AOA), and active language-use context, controlling for age, education, and sex. Longer L2 immersion duration was associated with stronger BOLD-CSF coupling (r = -.316, q = .029; two-tailed q = .059) and smaller ChP ratios (r = -.386, q = .016). An exploratory mediation analysis indicated an indirect association with the ALPS index through ChP ratio and BOLD-CSF coupling. AOA moderated the immersion-coupling association, significant among earlier learners (B = -.134, p < .001) but not later learners. AOA did not moderate the ChP association and ALPS index. Only active L2 use within immersive environments was associated with the markers, whereas passive immersion and non-immersive active use were not. L2 immersion duration is associated directly and indirectly with MRI-derived glymphatic-related markers in healthy adults. These findings extend research on bilingualism and brain health to glymphatic-related physiology and motivate longitudinal tests of whether this association contributes to cognitive reserve.

title: iNGR-Modified Brucine-Loaded Liposomes Enhance Tumor Penetration and Suppress Ovarian Cancer Peritoneal Metastasis.
abstract: To develop an iNGR peptide-modified PEGylated liposomal brucine formulation (iNGR-Bru-lip) for targeted treatment of ovarian cancer peritoneal metastasis and to evaluate its tumor targeting, penetration, antitumor activity, underlying mechanism, and biosafety. The iNGR peptide was conjugated to DSPE-PEG-NHS and incorporated into brucine-loaded liposomes. The formulation was characterized using cryogenic transmission electron microscopy, dynamic light scattering, zeta-potential analysis, encapsulation-efficiency measurement, stability testing, and in vitro drug-release assays. Cellular uptake and targeting specificity were evaluated using confocal microscopy, flow cytometry, competition assays, and receptor-blocking experiments. Antitumor activity, autophagy-related changes, and apoptosis were investigated using cellular assays, MDC staining, transmission electron microscopy, Western blotting, and EBSS-mediated autophagy activation. Biodistribution, tumor penetration, therapeutic efficacy, and systemic safety were assessed in an ES-2 peritoneal xenograft model. iNGR-Bru-lip displayed a uniform spherical morphology, an average diameter of 140.43 ± 0.64 nm, a polydispersity index below 0.15, negative surface charge, high brucine encapsulation efficiency (89.81 ± 2.50%), and stability for 30 days. The formulation exhibited sustained brucine release over 48 h. iNGR functionalization enhanced cellular uptake in CD13/NRP-1-high ES-2 cells, while competition with free iNGR peptide and CD13/NRP-1 blockade reduced cellular fluorescence. Compared with free brucine and non-targeted liposomes, iNGR-Bru-lip produced greater cytotoxicity, suppressed colony formation, migration, and invasion, and increased apoptosis. These effects were accompanied by autophagy-related changes, while EBSS-mediated autophagy activation attenuated the pro-apoptotic response. Intraperitoneal administration produced greater tumor accumulation than intravenous administration. In vivo, iNGR-Bru-lip penetrated peritoneal tumor tissues and significantly reduced abdominal circumference progression and tumor burden. Hematological, biochemical, and histopathological assessments revealed no evident systemic toxicity. iNGR-Bru-lip integrates combines receptor-associated targeting, enhanced tumor penetration, and autophagy-associated apoptosis induction, providing a promising nanomedicine strategy for ovarian cancer peritoneal metastasis.

title: Diagnosis provision by young people's mental health services: a population-based study in South London integrating epidemiological estimates.
abstract: Little is known about the provision of diagnoses to young people with mental health disorders. We investigated diagnosis provision by NHS mental health services, focusing on 17-year-olds in South London, UK, between 2009 and 2024, and compared with estimated disorder prevalence. We extracted diagnosis data from records of the NHS mental healthcare provider serving South London, using the Clinical Record Interactive Search system at the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre: Maudsley. We compared these data with three denominators: the population size, obtained from the Office for National Statistics; the number estimated to have met criteria for a mental health disorder, derived from epidemiological interview data collected in the Environmental Risk (E-Risk) Longitudinal Twin Study and weighted to characteristics of 17-year-old South Londoners; and the number estimated to have met criteria for a disorder and used any health service for their mental health, also from weighted E-Risk Study data. Of 17-year-olds from South London in 2009-2024, 4.0% (n = 8958/223,404) had a diagnosis in NHS mental health records during the previous year. This diagnosis provision covered <1 in 15 of those estimated to have had a disorder, and <1 in 4 of those estimated to have also used health services. Diagnosis provision was lower in girls than boys and in those with Black, Asian, Mixed, or Other ethnicity than their White peers, in those estimated to have had a disorder and used health services. These findings demonstrate gaps and biases in diagnosis provision by NHS mental health services for young people, including among those who had seen any health professional for help, and reveal the imperative need to strengthen young people's mental healthcare. National Institute for Health and Care Research, Medical Research Council, National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, Jacobs Foundation, National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, Economic and Social Research Council, Prudence Trust, King's College London, Wellcome Trust, Canadian Institute for Advanced Research.

title: MT2 melatonin receptor activation attenuates ferroptosis in OGD/R-induced HT22 cells via the GPX4/SLC7A11/p-ERK/Nrf2 antioxidant defense system.
abstract: Melatonin is widely recognized for its antioxidant and neuroprotective properties. However, the significant role of melatonin receptors (MT1/MT2) in regulating ferroptosis in ischemic stroke remains to be elucidated. In this study, we investigated whether melatonin attenuates ferroptosis-associated neurotoxicity in an oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) model using mouse hippocampal HT22 cells, with particular emphasis on receptor-dependent signaling. We observed OGD/R induced ferroptosis, evidenced by increased intracellular iron (Fe2 +), lipid peroxidation products (malondialdehyde (MDA), 4-hydroxynonenal (4HNE)), and reactive oxygen species (ROS), accompanied by suppression of the antioxidant defense system, glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11), and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) levels. Melatonin treatment significantly reduced these ferroptosis-associated neurotoxicity and restored the levels of key antioxidant regulators. Pharmacological inhibition of Nrf2 using ML385 abolished melatonin-induced upregulation of GPX4 and SLC7A11, confirming that its protective effects are Nrf2-dependent. Furthermore, blockade of melatonin receptors with luzindole and 4P-PDOT abolished these protective effects. Selective MT2 receptor blockade with 4P-PDOT also abolished the melatonin-induced increase in phosphorylated extracellular signal-regulated kinase (p-ERK), indicating a critical role for MT2 receptor signaling in regulating the cellular antioxidant defense system against ferroptosis under ischemic-like conditions. Collectively, these findings indicate that melatonin attenuates OGD/R-induced ferroptosis-neurotoxicity through an MT2 receptor-dependent mechanism, activating the antioxidant defense GPX4/SLC7A11/p-ERK/Nrf2 axis, supporting its potential relevance in ischemic neuroprotection.

title: AAIC 2026: Understanding dementia from the perspective of neurovascular pathology.
abstract: •A vascular ("V") dimension is needed beside ATN, with imaging and fluid biomarkers still requiring harmonization and prospective validation.•White matter changes reflect both vascular and neurodegenerative pathology, and separating these contributions is essential for trial eligibility, safety, and monitoring.•Diffusion MRI-based vascular features may be more responsive to intervention than conventional endpoints such as WMH.•Operational "V-positivity," earlier diffusion-based markers, and pathophysiology-based trial design are priorities for modifying cerebrovascular contributions to dementia.

title: EEG biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases: Machine learning applications and clinical trial insights.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) are diverse conditions characterised by selective dysfunction and progressive loss of neurons, glial cells, and neural networks in the brain and spinal cord. NDs pose a major global health challenge due to ageing populations and lack of cure, prompting interest in developing algorithms for early detection and biomarkers. Electroencephalography (EEG), a non-invasive and cost-effective tool, has emerged as a promising method for identifying neural signatures of NDs. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) have further enabled automated diagnosis, disease monitoring, and prognostic modelling using EEG data. This review synthesises evidence from 226 studies, mapping the current landscape of EEG-based diagnosis, prognosis, and patient stratification across various NDs. Unlike prior reviews, it provides a comprehensive overview across multiple disorders, including rare ones, and evaluates the role of ML and AI in clinical translation. We analyse research trends, EEG acquisition and preprocessing, and the development of biomarkers for disease diagnosis, prognosis, treatment monitoring, and patient stratification. Spectral power, event-related potentials, and connectivity are the main features, with support vector machines and neural networks as the primary classifiers. We review clinical trials involving EEG in NDs and highlight open-source EEG repositories to support reproducibility and data sharing. Despite promising results, challenges such as small sample sizes, methodological differences, limited model interpretability, and gaps in clinical validation remain. The review highlights the potential of EEG combined with ML/AI for early diagnosis and therapy, while outlining future directions through standardised pipelines, explainable models, and collaborative open data initiatives.

title: A review of glioblastoma 3D cell culture models: Properties and applications in drug screening.
abstract: Glioblastoma is classified as the most aggressive brain tumor due to its invasive nature and rapid progression. It is clinically treated using combinations of different chemotherapeutic agents, such as Temozolomide, Carmustine, and Lomustine, along with surgery and/or radiotherapy. GBM cells often develop resistance to traditional treatments, leading to a need for the development of new therapies. But due to the complexity of the tumor microenvironment and its limited representation in laboratory models, most newly developed drugs fail to pass clinical trials, highlighting the need for clinically relevant preclinical testing models. Clinically relevant models would incorporate GBM cells in a three-dimensional setting that mimics the in vivo cancer environment and include key features such as the tumor microenvironment and the blood-brain barrier. This narrative review aims to identify 3D cell culture protocols that incorporate the tumor into such an environment and to assess their potential as models for testing glioblastoma treatments. A comprehensive search on Google Scholar and PubMed using the keywords Glioblastoma organoids", "Brain Organoids", "Glioblastoma 3D cell culture", "Brain 3D cell culture", and "Advances in brain cell culture" was done to identify published research work. The PRISMA 2020 guidelines were used to select the papers. The inclusion of the scientific research articles into the study was based on the presence or absence of brain tumor organoids/spheroids and/or cerebral organoids. After shortlisting, 28 studies were analyzed for the review, and the extracted data were put in a Table. The co-culture of cerebral organoids with GBM cells or Glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs)-based spheroids was the most common protocol used in the studies (38%). 14.3% of the studies reported the in vitro establishment of the BBB, and 50% of these studies used bioprinting and microfluidics-based approaches. 68% of the total studies included patient-derived samples, and preservation of patient-specific heterogeneity in the 3D models was also reported. This literature review provides a detailed analysis and summary of the different 3D cell culture techniques that have been developed to study the in vitro effects of the TME and BBB on drug treatment. The findings of this review will help researchers gain a comprehensive understanding of the different types of 3D brain cell culture models, including their design, biological relevance, and translational potential. By critically evaluating current methodologies, applications, and limitations, this review provides a consolidated framework to guide model selection for neuroscience research, disease modelling, and drug screening. Furthermore, the insights presented may support the advancement of more physiologically relevant in vitro brain models and inform future research directions toward improved reproducibility and clinical translation.

title: BDNF-mediated amelioration of sleep disruption-induced behavioral disorders by Ginkgo biloba.
abstract: Sleep disruptions linked to adverse outcomes ranging from cognitive decline (e.g., in memory, learning, and sensory integration) to emotional dysregulation (e.g., stress and pathological anxiety). Although pre-sleep cognitive engagement may alleviate some of these effects, effective pharmacological interventions are needed. Ginkgo biloba, a dietary supplement, exerts broad pharmacological actions that support neural function. Here, we investigate hypothesis that Ginkgo biloba counteracts sleep deprivation's detrimental effects by promoting BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity, thereby restoring cognitive and emotional homeostasis. Twenty-eight male Wistar rats were randomly assigned to four groups: sleep disruption (SD) followed by Ginkgo biloba extract (250 mg/kg i.p.), sleep-disrupted group only, extract only, and control. The Ginkgo biloba collected from botanical garden of Tehran and the extract was prepared via percolation of plant material with ethanol, followed by evaporation and reconstitution. Animals were subjected to multiple-platform-induced sleep disruption (MPSD) for 2 h/day for 3 consecutive days. Behavioral assessments included the open-field test for stress/anxiety and the Barnes maze for spatial learning and memory over three days. Hippocampal BDNF levels were quantified using ELISA. Intraperitoneal Ginkgo biloba extract improved learning in sleep-disrupted rats, reducing probe-day latency from 71 ± 11 s (deprived) to 38 ± 8 s (p < 0.001); Ginkgo biloba alone yielded 15 ± 8 s. The open-field test revealed a significant increase in both locomotor speed and total distance traveled in the sleep-disrupted rats compared with the other experimental groups (P < 0.001). Sleep disruption reduced hippocampal BDNF from 544.55 ± 23-381.19 ± 17 pm/ml (p < 0.0001). Ginkgo biloba treatment significantly prevented this reduction (557 ± 27 pm/ml; p < 0.001) and, when administered alone, increased BDNF by 20% compared to controls (653 ± 25 pm/ml). Sleep disruption impaired memory and learning but did not significantly affect anxiety. Treatment with Ginkgo biloba extract (250 mg/kg) improved memory and reduced anxiety. Hippocampal BDNF changes suggest restorative effects may be mediated by increasing BDNF levels reduced by deprivation. As an Iranian Ginkgo biloba extract was used, further research is needed to identify optimal extraction methods and phytochemical compositions for enhancing BDNF levels, thereby optimizing therapeutic potential of Ginkgo biloba -derived compounds for sleep and cognitive applications.

title: Electrode-Based Neuromodulation for Refractory Painful Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy: A Narrative Review of Current Evidence and Clinical Integration.
abstract: Painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy (PDPN) is a complex, progressive complication characterized by small-fiber degeneration, microvascular insufficiency, metabolic stress, and maladaptive central sensitization. First-line medications are generally only partially effective and frequently provide incomplete or insufficiently durable relief, underscoring the importance of mechanism-based interventions. This narrative review was based on searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library from database inception through 2026, with priority given to English-language studies involving human subjects. The evidence was narratively synthesized and appraised by experts rather than systematically pooled, and no meta-analysis was performed. Neuromodulation directly modulates dysfunctional nociceptive circuits through approaches such as peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS), dorsal root ganglion stimulation (DRGS), and spinal cord stimulation (SCS). These emerging treatments may also provide microvascular and neuroimmune benefits. High-frequency and burst SCS provide nonparesthetic analgesia through mechanisms more congruent with endogenous pain-modulatory physiology, whereas closed-loop SCS based on evoked compound action potentials (ECAPs) enables real-time, stable engagement of neural tissue. Recent improvements in wireless platforms, miniaturized micro-electrode systems, and regenerative stimulation have increased therapeutic applications and decreased procedural burden while improving neural selectivity. Neuromodulation is progressing toward personalized, adaptive treatment through data-driven optimization of stimulation parameters and phenotype-specific programming, facilitated by artificial intelligence (AI). Biomarker-guided patient selection using quantitative sensory testing, intra-epidermal nerve fiber density, electrophysiologic measures, and advanced imaging is proposed as a framework for aligning therapeutic modality with disease phenotype. However, no biomarker has yet been validated to predict response to neuromodulation in PDPN, and this stratification remains hypothesis-generating and has not been prospectively validated. Neuromodulation is emerging as a mechanism-targeted and increasingly individualized approach for refractory PDPN that can provide sustained pain relief and functional benefits when other treatments have been ineffective. Preliminary evidence also suggests possible disease-modifying properties, although these require confirmation in PDPN-specific, long-term comparative trials.

title: Chaperone-mediated autophagy targets Miro-1 for degradation to promote mitophagy and inhibit α-synuclein induced ferroptosis.
abstract: Ferroptotic neurodegeneration has emerged as a key pathological driver in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the upstream mechanisms that connect α-synuclein pathology to ferroptosis remain poorly defined. To delineate how pathological α-synuclein triggers mitochondria-associated ferroptosis via chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) inhibition, and to develop targeted approaches for intervening in ferroptotic neurodegeneration. α-Synuclein pathology was modeled using pre-formed fibrils (PFFs) in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells and A53T transgenic mice. Ferroptosis, mitophagy and CMA were assessed using biochemical, imaging and genetic approaches. A midbrain-targeted acoustically activatable liposomal formulation loaded with the CMA agonist CA77.1 (AAL-CA) was engineered to achieve site-specific CMA activation in vivo. We found that α-synuclein pathology induced ferroptosis and impaired mitophagy in PD models. Mechanistically, α-synuclein stress suppressed CMA activity, resulting in Miro-1 accumulation by impairing its degradation. Accumulated Miro-1 competed with PINK1 for binding to TOMM70, thereby inhibiting PINK1-Parkin-mediated mitophagy. Genetic manipulation of Miro-1 levels, combined with pharmacological modulation of CMA, demonstrated that Miro-1 accumulation is both sufficient and necessary to inhibit mitophagy and ferroptosis under α-synuclein stress. Midbrain-targeted AAL-CA activated CMA, reduced Miro-1 levels, restored mitophagy, inhibited ferroptosis, preserved dopaminergic neurons, and improved motor deficits in A53T mice. Collectively, CMA dysfunction links α-synuclein pathology to ferroptosis via Miro-1-dependent mitophagy impairment. Targeted CMA activation is a promising disease-modifying approach for PD.

title: Can the Quality of Peripheral Nerve Regeneration Influence the Development of Chronic Postsurgical Pain?
abstract: Chronic postsurgical pain (CPSP) is a multifactorial condition that may arise from persistent nociceptive input, peripheral and central sensitization, and neuroimmune mechanisms. Peripheral nerve injury can initiate Wallerian degeneration, Schwann-cell reprogramming, immune-cell recruitment, and axonal regeneration. However, whether the quality of nerve regeneration influences long-term postsurgical pain remains uncertain. This narrative review examines the potential relationship between peripheral nerve regeneration, functional target reinnervation, and persistent postsurgical pain while distinguishing established repair mechanisms from hypotheses about pain persistence. A focused narrative literature review was conducted. Literature was initially identified on September 27, 2026, through Google and PubMed searches and was supplemented by topic-specific and reference-based searches. Peripheral nerve repair involves coordinated interactions among axons, Schwann cells, immune cells, and the local microenvironment. Axonal regrowth alone does not ensure functional recovery; accurate target reinnervation and restoration of sensory or motor function are also important. Experimental studies suggest that regenerating axons, particularly when appropriate target reinnervation fails, may be associated with abnormal sensory activity and persistent pain-related behaviors. Schwann cell and neuroimmune signaling may also modulate nociceptive responses. Nevertheless, much of this evidence is derived from animal nerve-injury models and does not directly establish the mechanisms of chronic postsurgical pain (CPSP) in humans. Clinical studies of targeted muscle reinnervation and regenerative peripheral nerve interfaces have primarily examined neuroma-related and postamputation pain. Their reported pain outcomes do not, by themselves, demonstrate that improved nerve regeneration mediates analgesia or that these approaches prevent CPSP across other surgical populations. Evidence concerning mesenchymal stromal cell-derived extracellular vesicles remains predominantly preclinical. Peripheral nerve regeneration may be one component of the biological processes relevant to persistent postsurgical pain, but its independent contribution to CPSP has not been established. Functional recovery and persistent pain may coexist, and the predictive value of measurable regeneration characteristics remains unknown. Prospective clinical studies are needed to determine whether the quality of nerve repair is associated with long-term pain outcomes after surgery.

title: Dynamical mechanisms of pathological phase-amplitude coupling in a network comprising subthalamic and two types of globus pallidus neurons.
abstract: Pathologically enhanced β oscillations and their cross-frequency coupling with high-frequency oscillations is a hallmark of Parkinson's disease, yet its dynamical origins remain elusive, partly due to oversimplified modeling of the GPe as a homogeneous nucleus. In this study, we developed a biophysical STN-heterogeneous GPe network model incorporating prototypic (TI) and arkypallidal (TA) neurons to investigate the phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) generation and the differential roles of intra-loop pathways. Our results show that the STN-TI-STN sub-loop serves as the core dynamical substrate for generating and sustaining pathological PAC. TA neurons do not drive PAC but potentiate it via lateral inhibition onto TI, with their drive originating from STN input. Selective TI excitation abolishes PAC, whereas TA stimulation is ineffective. The consistent evolution of synchronization index, β power, and modulation index supports PAC as a reliable feedback biomarker. This work points to a new network mechanism of PAC generation within the STN-heterogeneous GPe network, identifies the TI subpopulation as a promising target for precision optogenetic intervention, and provides theoretical foundations for developing adaptive DBS strategies guided by PAC-based feedback signals.

title: Public Reporting Completeness of Medicare Remote Monitoring Services: A Retrospective Observational Study.
abstract: Background and objective Remote patient monitoring (RPM) uses physiologic measurements, while remote therapeutic monitoring (RTM) tracks nonphysiologic information such as symptoms and therapy adherence. Public Medicare provider files support studies of these services, but privacy-related suppression can affect service counts and provider representation differently. This study aimed to quantify reporting completeness against separately aggregated Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) national and state reference data. Methods This was a retrospective observational study with descriptive analyses that compared the CMS Medicare Physician and Other Practitioners provider-and-service and geography-and-service files for 2019-2024. The primary analysis was 2024. Service completeness was the provider-file service sum divided by the corresponding geographic total. Provider-cell completeness compared disclosed rendering-provider-code-setting records with reference counts in the same strata. RPM included 99453, 99454, 99457, and 99458 when available; RTM included 98975-98978, 98980, and 98981 when available. Code 99091 was analyzed separately. Missing reference cells remained non-estimable. Historical, state, payment, and fixed-code nonfacility analyses assessed sensitivity. Results The extraction contained 77,895 provider records and 2,395 geographic records across 46 code-years. In 2024, the provider file retained 6,780,279 of 7,217,550 RPM service units (93.94%) but 21,311 of 59,185 provider-code-setting cells (36.01%). For RTM, it retained 482,639 of 547,840 units (88.10%) and 2,996 of 17,519 cells (17.10%) across published national reference strata. Service shortfalls were 437,271 for RPM and 65,201 for RTM. Code-specific RTM service completeness ranged from 76.67% to 99.31%, whereas cell completeness ranged from 13.76% to 28.29%. Median jurisdiction-level service completeness was 91.12% for RPM (51 jurisdictions) and 82.24% for RTM (48 jurisdictions). In a sensitivity analysis restricted to five fixed nonfacility RTM codes, 2022-2024 growth was 866.79% in provider data versus 804.51% in geographic data. No published national facility denominator was available for 98978 in 2024. Conclusions Public provider data retained most remote-monitoring service units while omitting a much larger share of provider-code-setting records. Cell-completeness percentages do not estimate the proportion of unique providers represented. Reporting completeness varied by code, geography, and year. Studies should reconcile aggregation levels and avoid interpreting absent public records as nonuse, limited patient access, or lack of clinical benefit.

title: Playing with the dials of belief: how controllable AI behaviours could modulate human belief and cognition across scales.
abstract: Contemporary generative AI systems, increasingly adapted to human social cognition, are becoming active participants in how people form and revise beliefs. Clinicians have begun to describe AI-associated delusion-centred presentations whose onset or content appears closely associated with users' extended dialogue with large language models. Many more users report subclinical shifts in conviction and "revelatory" experiences that alter behaviour and world-view without meeting criteria for psychosis. We propose that these phenomena can be understood within a belief-updating framework in which AI agents' outputs function as testimony about the world, while interaction configurations, such as memory and interpersonal stance (many of which reflect design choices or deployment defaults), can alter the apparent reliability of that testimony and the precision users assign to it. On this view, AI-associated delusions sit at the extreme of a broader spectrum of epistemic effects, extending from gradual epistemic drift to highly crystallised conviction, situated within a wider ecology of belief shaped by personalised human-AI dyads. We develop a virtual psychopharmacology analogy in which different AI system configurations have effects on belief dynamics that resemble neuromodulatory changes in the precision assigned to social evidence. We also consider how dopaminergic and related states may alter susceptibility to belief-shifting dialogue. We consider how deliberately configured agents might be used to support wellbeing in defined clinical contexts and analyse how the same configurations could be deployed to shape belief and attention at population scale, including in products designed to induce spiritual or epiphanic states, as mechanisms of radicalisation in extremist or cultic contexts, and in persona clones used for political purposes. We conclude that interaction configurations should be treated as modifiable influences on belief and attention, and that governance must address both the concentration of control over these dials, as well as the structural biases that determine whose testimonial perspectives are amplified and whose are smoothed over or ignored.

title: Inferotemporal cortex stimulation is perceived before its onset.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Neural response latency measures when stimulus-evoked activity becomes detectable, but it does not reveal when the brain assigns the causal contribution of that activity to events in the external world. We define this temporal adjustment as projected delay and measure it in the macaque inferotemporal cortex using optogenetic stimulation and behavior. Two rhesus macaques performed a cortical perturbation detection task in which a visual masker appeared at different times relative to stimulation. Detection was selectively impaired when the masker began 200 ms before stimulation. We then tested this timing using Perceptography, a method that optimizes image perturbations to mimic stimulation-evoked visual events. Image perturbations presented 200 ms before stimulation elicited higher false-alarm rates than perturbations presented at stimulation onset. Here, we show that stimulation-evoked visual events in inferotemporal cortex depend preferentially on visual information originating approximately 200 ms before the cortical perturbation. This projected delay exceeds typical inferotemporal response latencies and suggests temporally extended readout mechanisms relevant to causal models of visual perception and the timing of cortical visual prostheses.

title: SALRR: Scalable Analysis of Long-Read RNA-Seq Enables Comprehensive Transcriptome Profiling in Human Brain.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Isoform-resolved transcriptomics is fundamental to decoding the molecular complexity of the human brain, yet population-scale long-read RNA sequencing has remained inaccessible due to labor-intensive library preparation, sensitivity to RNA degradation in postmortem tissue, and the absence of integrated, reproducible analysis pipelines. Here we present SALRR (Scalable Analysis of Long-Read RNA-seq), an integrated wet-lab and computational platform designed to overcome these barriers. Automated ONT long-read cDNA library preparation on the Hamilton Microlab NGS STAR platform reduces hands-on time by 67% and enables 24 libraries per operator per day while maintaining performance across RNA integrity values. A modular, Snakemake-based pipeline performs end-to-end processing from ONT signal data to isoform-level quantification, incorporating SIRV spike-in calibration, multi-stage quality control, and stringent isoform validation. Applied to 10 postmortem frontal cortex samples from the North American Brain Expression Consortium, SALRR identified 31,607 high-confidence isoforms from 10,075 genes, including 8,532 novel splice variants absent from GENCODE v49, and complex splicing events systematically missed by short-read sequencing at neurodegeneration-relevant loci, including GBA1 , CCNF , CHCHD10 , and TREM2 . All protocols and code are openly available, providing a scalable, community-ready framework for isoform-resolved transcriptomics in neurodegeneration, aging, and complex brain disease.

title: Lifespan brain structural variation reveals shared organization across mental health conditions.
authors: van der Wee Nic J A
journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
abstract: Elucidating the neurobiological basis of neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions (NDPCs) remains challenging because brain alterations vary within diagnoses and overlap across them. Whether diverse alterations follow a systematic organization that may reflect shared vulnerabilities remains unknown. Here, we assembled 10,135 individuals with schizophrenia, autism, bipolar, obsessive-compulsive, generalized anxiety, and major depressive disorders, and 11,998 reference participants across six continents through the ENIGMA consortium. Using normative modeling, we quantified individual deviations in cortical thickness, surface area, and subcortical volumes relative to lifespan reference trajectories (5 to 80 years). We show that structural deviations converged along cortical axes reflecting connectome organization, maturation, and cytoarchitectonic diversity. These axes mirrored typical population variation, but their expression differed across diagnoses and partly scaled with symptom severity. Even rare and highly individualized extreme deviations followed this organization, concentrating in densely connected regions. Finally, brain structural deviations overlapped substantially across diagnoses, while differences between them increased toward the association cortex. Together, we provide large-scale evidence that structural deviations across NDPCs are systematically constrained by the brain's intrinsic architecture. This shared organization provides a framework for reconciling individual variability with transdiagnostic similarities and motivates an integrative, systems-level understanding of mental health.

title: Continuous Rod Noise and Nonlinear Synaptic Filtering Shape Signal Detection in the Primary Rod Pathway.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Rod photoreceptors are optimized to detect single photons, but their performance near absolute visual threshold is limited by intrinsic phototransduction noise. The two major components are discrete single-photon-like events and continuous fluctuations in outer-segment current. Although spontaneous rhodopsin activation is established as the source of discrete noise, the molecular origin of continuous noise remains controversial, and how these distinct noise sources influence signal processing at the first visual synapse is not fully understood. To address these questions, we combined genetic manipulation of rhodopsin, phosphodiesterase 6 (PDE6), and glutamic acid rich protein 2 (GARP2) with single-cell recordings from rods and rod-bipolar cells (RBCs) and pharmacological manipulation of mGluR6 signaling. Continuous noise was unaffected by reduced rhodopsin concentration but was strongly influenced by PDE6 expression and regulation, supporting basal PDE6 activity as a major source of continuous noise. Reducing either discrete or continuous noise increased signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in rods, but these changes were differentially processed at the rod-to-RBC synapse. In WT retina, the nonlinear transformation increased SNR, whereas elevated continuous noise limited this increase. Conversely, reduced continuous noise increased rod SNR, which was maintained in RBCs and associated with a lower detection threshold. Pharmacological reduction of the mGluR6-dependent nonlinearity altered these genotype-dependent differences, indicating that nonlinear filtering is well matched to normal signal and noise distributions but does not fully compensate when presynaptic noise is experimentally altered. Together, our study identifies spontaneous PDE6 activity as a major source of continuous noise and demonstrates that continuous noise interacts with nonlinear processing at the first visual synapse to determine the fidelity and detection threshold of dim-light signals. Vision near absolute threshold requires retinal circuits to distinguish single-photon responses from intrinsic photoreceptor noise. We show that basal PDE6 activity is a major source of continuous noise in rod photoreceptors and that altering this noise affects signal fidelity after convergence onto rod bipolar cells. Nonlinear filtering at the first visual synapse interacts with presynaptic noise levels, while reducing continuous rod noise improves the detection of near-threshold light signals. These findings link the molecular mechanisms generating photoreceptor noise to its processing by downstream retinal circuitry and demonstrate how noise control at both cellular and synaptic levels contributes to the remarkable sensitivity of the primary rod pathway.

title: MIND the gap: methodological considerations and guidance for structural MRI similarity network analysis with MIND.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Structural similarity networks quantify the similarity of structural properties across cortical regions, providing a macroscopic window onto the organisation of cortical architecture. Morphometric inverse divergence (MIND) is a multivariate metric of similarity between cortical areas, based on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between areal distributions of multiple MRI features or morphometric variables locally measured at voxel or vertex resolution. MIND has demonstrated technical robustness and biological validity and is increasingly widely used as a measure of cortico-cortical similarity in clinical and developmental network neuroscience. Here we provide in-depth methodological background on KL divergence and MIND, highlighting possible sources of bias, critical user decision points in the design of a MIND processing pipeline, and recommendations for technical risk mitigation in using MIND as a metric of cortical similarity. We use simulated data and observational MRI datasets from adults (UK Biobank, N = 500 T1-weighted and diffusion scans) and neonates (Developing Human Connectome Project, N = 752 T2-weighted scans), to show how the estimator of KL divergence implemented in MIND is potentially influenced or biased by five properties of input MRI feature maps: (i) their smoothness; (ii) the proportion of identical values; (iii) analysis in native or common space and the choice of vertex mesh resolution; (iv) parcellation choice; and (v) covariance between input features. We offer principled and practical guidance for investigators wanting to specify and implement the MIND processing pipeline that is best suited to the constraints and opportunities of the MRI data available to them. These recommendations outline which pipeline steps should be used sparingly, such as vertex map smoothing; which should be used with informed caution, such as parcellation choice or vertex mesh resampling; and which could be newly implemented for more robust estimation of MIND, such as the use of principal component analysis to preprocess multivariate MRI features. To support further development of structural MRI similarity network analysis, and wider adoption of robust MIND methods, we also publish the code used to generate the results in this paper as an open resource.

title: Edge controllability is associated with treatment response to repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in depression.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is an established treatment for major depressive disorder (MDD), yet variability in treatment response remains a significant challenge. Network control theory provides a framework to quantify how brain networks facilitate state transitions, but prior work has focused primarily on node level metrics. Here, I investigate whether edge based controllability of the structural connectome is associated with rTMS outcomes. Twenty five patients with treatment-resistant depression underwent diffusion MRI prior to a five week course of high frequency rTMS targeting the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Structural connectomes were constructed using MRtrix3 and the Destrieux atlas, and edge based controllability metrics were computed at baseline. Controllability of specific middle frontal gyrus centered edges showed significant associations with changes in HAMD-24 scores, including connections to the superior frontal gyrus, hippocampus, angular gyrus, and orbital gyrus (r = -(0.470-0.597), p < 0.05). These findings suggest that edge based controllability captures circuit level properties relevant to treatment response and may inform personalized neuromodulation strategies.

title: A reactivated thalamocortical plasticity window promotes learning and is reshaped by experience.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Adult sensory loss can reactivate critical-period-like thalamocortical plasticity, but whether this reactivation defines a temporally gated circuit state that facilitates learning and is reciprocally shaped by experience remains unknown. Here we define its in vivo trajectory and functional consequences in adult mouse barrel cortex. Infraorbital nerve transection opened a transient window of enhanced layer 4 thalamocortical gain. Training during this window lowered whisker-detection thresholds and promoted learning by accelerating the transition to stable performance. Local GluN2B blockade prevented both cortical potentiation and the learning advantage, linking critical-period-associated plasticity mechanisms to adaptive behavior in the adult brain. Neuropixels recordings showed that weak inputs preferentially increased neuronal responses, whereas strong inputs produced sharper temporal coding. The relationship was reciprocal: experience reshaped the trajectory of this circuit state, with training before the normal peak advancing the emergence of potentiation, training during the active window prolonging the potentiated state, and training after closure failing to reinstate potentiation. State prolongation accompanied more persistent sensory memory. These findings establish a reciprocal, timing-dependent interaction between endogenous plasticity and experience, revealing a general principle by which adult circuits can convert transient plastic potential into adaptive behavioral change and informing strategies that align training with periods of heightened plasticity.

title: Direct convective delivery for gene therapy targeting central nervous system disorders.
journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy
abstract: Advances in the molecular biologic understanding of neurologic diseases have led to the development of targeted gene therapies for previously incompletely treatable or untreatable nervous system disorders. Intraparenchymal convection-enhanced delivery (CED) is the most common method for viral vector delivery in nervous system gene therapy trials. The expanding use of convective delivery underscores the need to understand its benefits, limitations and technical prerequisites. Convective delivery uses a small hydrostatic pressure gradient to drive bulk flow of infusate through the interstitial space, enabling predictable, homogeneous distribution within targeted structures, bypassing the blood-brain barrier. Coupling CED with viral vector biology (defined cellular tropism and directional axonal transport) enables widespread, circuit-targeted treatment beyond the infusion site. Real-time imaging with a co-infused surrogate tracer allows for visualization of infusate distribution, detection of off-target perfusion, correlation with transgene expression and perfusion optimization (e.g., adjusting flow rates, cannula position or stopping infusion). Standardized infusion protocols, stereotactic cannula placement and advanced imaging modalities underscore the reproducibility of CED. The reproducibility and anatomic precision of convective delivery distinguish it from alternative approaches. As convective delivery of gene therapies moves toward regulatory approval, the standardization and scalability of this platform are promising factors that can significantly enhance therapeutic outcomes.

title: Bidirectional Relations Between Spirituality and Adolescent Depression and Anxiety: The Moderating Role of Religious Involvement.
abstract: Typically, spirituality is viewed as a protective factor against mental health challenges. But it is possible that inversely mental health challenges are a risk factor for hindered spirituality. This study examined longitudinal bidirectional relations between spirituality and adolescent depression and anxiety, and the moderating role of religious involvement. Participants included 1862 adolescents from the western US (Time 2 Mage = 16; 53% female; 77% European American). Adolescents completed self-report measures of spirituality, depression, anxiety, and religious involvement across three waves, 2 years apart. Bidirectional relations between adolescent spirituality and mental health were examined using Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models (RI-CLPM). Analyses revealed that at the within-person level, spirituality did not significantly predict later depression, but depression did negatively predict later spirituality. Additionally, spirituality negatively predicted subsequent anxiety, and anxiety negatively predicted later spirituality. The model was also tested across two groups based on the level of religious involvement, comparing those who attended religious worship services less than weekly to those who attended at least weekly. Bidirectional within-person associations between spirituality and mental health were found for frequent attenders but not infrequent attenders (for both depression and anxiety). These findings suggest potential bidirectional dynamics between adolescent spirituality and mental health, especially for religiously engaged youth.

title: Longitudinal plasma proteomic signatures following lecanemab treatment in patients with Alzheimer's disease.
journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
abstract: Amyloid-targeting therapies have shifted Alzheimer's disease management toward biomarker-guided monitoring, yet the amyloid/tau/neurodegeneration (ATN) biomarker framework does not fully capture molecular responses to amyloid clearance. Longitudinal plasma proteomic changes during lecanemab treatment have not been characterized. A total of 112 participants were enrolled: 67 amyloid beta (Aβ)-positive patients receiving lecanemab (LEC), 30 Aβ-positive participants not receiving lecanemab (Ctrl A+), and 15 Aβ-negative controls (Ctrl A-). Participants contributed 229 clinical visits over up to 18 months, of which 209 plasma samples from 95 participants were included in the current NULISAseq proteomic analysis. Between-group proteomic comparisons with the control groups were restricted to the common baseline-to-12-month interval. Plasma proteins were quantified using the NULISAseq CNS Disease Panel. Three groups were age-balanced (p = 0.718); LEC and Ctrl A+ had comparable Mini-Mental State Examination and Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores (p = 0.650 and 0.568), while both Aβ-positive groups showed more severe cognitive impairment than Ctrl A- (p < 0.001). Proteomic screening identified 44 time-dependent proteins, of which 37 exhibited 12-month within-treatment changes; 22 and 18 proteins changed relative to Ctrl A+ and Ctrl A-. The intersection of these analyses yielded a candidate 12-protein signature comprising acetylcholinesterase (ACHE), Aβ40, Aβ42, C-C motif chemokine ligand 3 (CCL3), C-C motif chemokine ligand 4 (CCL4), colony-stimulating factor 2 (CSF2), intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM1), interleukin-12 p70 (IL12p70), interleukin-16 (IL16), kinase insert domain receptor (KDR), triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2), and 14-3-3 protein zeta/delta (YWHAZ). Network analyses linked these proteins to amyloid biology, myeloid activation, chemokine-cytokine signaling, endothelial regulation, and synaptic/cholinergic pathways. ACHE correlated with clinical severity, cognition, and amyloid positron emission tomography burden. Early IL16 and IL12p70 changes showed exploratory associations with subsequent clinical trajectories. Lecanemab treatment was accompanied by plasma proteomic changes beyond canonical ATN markers, providing candidate plasma markers for treatment-response monitoring.

title: Dual-DUBTACs Enable Targeted Protein Stabilization via Multi-DUB Engagement.
abstract: Targeted protein stabilization has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy for restoring the abundance and function of disease-relevant proteins. Deubiquitinase-targeting chimeras (DUBTACs) offer a chemical approach to protein stabilization by recruiting deubiquitinases (DUBs) to promote target deubiquitination. However, current DUBTAC strategies generally rely on the recruitment of a single DUB, leaving the potential of engaging multiple DUBs through a common recruiter largely unexplored. Here, we report a dual-DUBTAC strategy that enables targeted protein stabilization through the recruitment of two distinct DUBs. Using Degrasyn, a small-molecule reversible covalent inhibitor of multiple DUBs, as a privileged scaffold, we engineered small molecules that selectively stabilize CFTR and cGAS and demonstrate that these compounds enhance target protein homeostasis through USP9X- and USP5-mediated deubiquitination in cells. By decoupling substrate stabilization from reliance on a single DUB, the Dual-DUB platform confers adaptability across diverse ubiquitin chain architectures and rewired proteostasis networks characteristic of heterogeneous tumors and could overcome potential drug resistance in future clinical applications. This strategy expands the chemical space for restoring protective proteins and establishes a general framework for functional reactivation of destabilized tumor-suppressive pathways.

title: XuanYu TongJing Tang alleviates depressive-like behaviors in LPS-induced mice: involvement of PI3K-AKT and MAPK signaling pathways.
abstract: Depression is a severe neuropsychiatric disorder involving neuroinflammation and impaired neuroplasticity. XuanYu TongJing Tang (XYTJT) is a classical Chinese herbal formula documented in Fu Qingzhu Nvke. It was originally indicated for menstrual irregularities, chronic pelvic inflammatory disease, endometritis, and dysfunctional uterine bleeding, and it has also been applied clinically to mood disorders. However, whether XYTJT exerts direct antidepressant efficacy remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the antidepressant effects and molecular mechanisms of XYTJT using an integrated systems pharmacology approach. The antidepressant efficacy of XYTJT was evaluated in mice with lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced depressive-like behaviors through behavioral tests, histopathology, and biochemical assays. Network pharmacology, transcriptomics-CMap analysis, and molecular dynamics simulations were employed to predict core targets and pathways, followed by experimental validation via Western blot and RT-qPCR. XYTJT pretreatment attenuated LPS-induced behavioral alterations, reduced hippocampal neuronal damage, elevated IL-10, and upregulated BDNF, TrkB, and PSD95. Notably, sucrose preference was not significantly altered among the groups. Network pharmacology identified 323 intersecting targets, with PIK3CA, AKT1, MAPK1, and MAPK3 enriched in PI3K-AKT and MAPK pathways, confirmed by transcriptomics-CMap. Benzoyloxypaeoniflorin, identified as a candidate neuroprotective component, showed concentration-dependent neuroprotection and stable binding to PI3K, AKT1, and MAPK3 in molecular dynamics simulations. These findings suggest that XYTJT attenuates LPS-induced depressive-like behavioral alterations, potentially through modulation of the PI3K-AKT-GSK3β and MAPK-ERK-CREB1 axes and suppression of STAT3-mediated neuroinflammation. Further studies with pharmacological inhibitors or genetic approaches are needed to confirm causality.

title: Motor pre-selection modulates action observation effects in sensorimotor cortices: a MEG study.
abstract: According to the Motor Simulation theory, observing an action automatically activates matching motor representations. This can explain why, in automatic imitation tasks, responses are faster when the observed action matches the required one, compared to when it differs. However, the automatic imitation task setting represents a very peculiar situation where participants need to pre-select the motor representations corresponding to the actions that they might observe, a situation quite different from daily-life contexts such as sports (e.g., tennis or basketball) where actions pre-selected for output are typically different from those observed, and where imitation errors or tendencies are seldom observed. This leads to the following question: Does the motor cortex response to observed actions depend on whether they match the motor representations pre-selected for output? In the present magnetoencephalography experiment, we studied, within the hand-related primary sensorimotor cortex, the oscillatory dynamics produced by the observation of hand actions in two conditions: either while participants pre-selected motor representations similar to those observed, or while they pre-selected markedly different motor representations, such as those involved in feet actions. Our data show that the motor cortex reacts differently to action observation in the two pre-selection conditions: alpha- and beta-band activity showed stronger desynchronization when the pre-selection involved motor representations matching those observed compared to non-matching ones. Specifically, observing hand actions while pre-selecting non-matching feet movements elicited a late rebound-like increase in alpha- and beta-band activity that was not observed when hand actions were pre-selected.

title: LOCALIZED shoulder fatigue alters early movement scaling during learning of Upper-Limb orientation.
abstract: Neuromuscular fatigue alters force-generating capacity and sensorimotor information, yet its consequences for motor learning remain unclear. We examined whether practicing goal-directed shoulder abduction under localized muscle fatigue altered angular endpoint accuracy and early movement velocity at acquisition and delayed retention. Forty healthy adults were randomly assigned to the Fatigue or Control group (n = 20 each). Objective performance fatigability and perceived fatigue were monitored. Retention was assessed one week later, first without fatigue and then under re-induced shoulder fatigue. Angular errors were quantified after an initial ballistic phase and after proprioceptive repositioning. Angular velocity 100 ms after movement onset reflected early, predominantly feedforward, movement production. Both groups reduced absolute and constant angular errors during acquisition. However, early angular velocity increased less during fatigued practice, and lower values in the Fatigue group persisted during non-fatigued retention at all target angles. Final absolute angular error was also higher in the Fatigue group during non-fatigued retention. Between-group differences were not detected during fatigued retention. These findings identify a retained change in how the shoulder movement was produced, within the limits of a simple single-joint angular movement and the fixed retention order.

title: A multimodal imaging framework for characterizing chronic neuropathology after traumatic brain injury.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is associated with progressive neurodegeneration, including chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), yet the spatiotemporal evolution of post-traumatic structural and molecular pathology remains incompletely understood. Conventional neuroimaging approaches have limited sensitivity for detecting the subtle microstructural and molecular alterations underlying chronic post-traumatic degeneration. Here, we established a multimodal molecular imaging framework in murine models of single and repetitive mild TBI by integrating high-field 9.4 T micro-MRI/diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) with multitracer PET-CT using 18F-FDG, 11C-PIB, and 18FS16. This approach enabled the in vivo assessment of white matter integrity, cerebral glucose metabolism, amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition, and tau accumulation. Imaging findings were further validated using molecular, histopathological, and behavioral analyses. MRI-DTI revealed widespread white matter abnormalities and hippocampal degeneration following repetitive mild TBI, while PET imaging demonstrated persistent cerebral hypometabolism accompanied by increased Aβ and tau deposition. These pathological alterations were further associated with sustained neuroinflammatory activation and cognitive impairment. Notably, correlation analyses among the PET metrics revealed inverse associations between cerebral glucose metabolism (18F-FDG) and both Aβ (11C-PIB) and tau (18FS16) accumulation, with a stronger association observed between 18F-FDG and 11C-PIB. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that integrated MRI-DTI and multitracer PET provide complementary characterization of structural, metabolic, and proteinopathic alterations following TBI. This multimodal framework provides a preclinical platform for investigating post-traumatic neurodegeneration and may facilitate the development and translational evaluation of imaging biomarkers for TBI.

title: Functional transcriptomic profile of mouse controlled cortical impact model of post-traumatic epilepsy with robust spontaneous recurrent seizures.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of acquired epilepsy, yet the molecular changes linking the initial injury to post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE) remain incompletely understood. Here, we used a severe controlled cortical impact mouse model that develops robust spontaneous recurrent seizures to characterize the temporal and regional progression of post-traumatic transcriptional responses. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed on the contralateral cortex and hippocampus collected from TBI and time-matched sham mice at 7, 21, and 60 days after injury, corresponding to the acute injury, latent period, and chronic epilepsy phases, respectively. Transcriptomic changes were characterized using differentially expressed gene (DEG) analysis, Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes gene-set enrichment analyses, and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. Transcriptomic responses were strongly dependent on brain region and disease phase. At 7 days, the cortex showed enhanced neuronal and structural signaling alongside suppression of immune, metabolic, and cell-cycle processes, whereas the hippocampus showed prominent neuroimmune activation and metabolic stress. By 21 days, before the emergence of spontaneous seizures, the hippocampus shifted toward partial normalization of metabolic pathway enrichment, accompanied by suppression of neurotransmission, synaptic plasticity, and neuronal organization. In contrast, the cortex showed increased enrichment of immune and tissue-remodeling processes. Although relatively few DEGs were detected at 60 days, a selective hippocampal signature persisted after PTE was established. Pathway analyses converged on coordinated changes in neuroimmune, metabolic, lipid-regulatory, and synaptic processes. Upstream Regulator Analysis further identified a temporal reversal in APOE-associated regulatory activity, linking inflammatory and lipid-metabolic responses with later synaptic remodeling. The 21-day post-injury hippocampus represents a critical disease-modification window. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PTE progression involves phase-specific molecular remodeling that shifts from an early cortical response to sustained hippocampal dysregulation. The latent hippocampal signature identifies a potentially actionable molecular window before recurrent seizure onset.

title: Intrasegmental and propriospinal phrenic circuit interneurons in intact CNS and following cervical spinal cord injury.
abstract: Cervical spinal cord injury disrupts descending respiratory circuitry, resulting in debilitating and often persistent ventilatory deficits. Respiratory drive emerges within medulla from the rostral ventral respiratory group, whose neurons project to C3-C6 phrenic motor neurons (PhMNs), which then innervate diaphragm, the primary muscle of inspiration. Though rostral ventral respiratory group neurons make extensive monosynaptic connection with PhMNs, this input can also be relayed through phrenic circuit interneurons (PC-INs) via polysynaptic pathways. However, the neuroanatomical connectivity between PC-INs and PhMNs remains incompletely understood. In both uninjured rats and the C2 hemisection model of cervical spinal cord injury, we performed tracing of interneurons that were part of the circuitry connected to PhMNs located in rostral (C3-C4) or caudal (C5-C6) portions of the phrenic nucleus by unilaterally injecting retrograde trans-synaptic tracer, pseudorabies virus, selectively into ventral or dorsal regions of hemidiaphragm. We quantified numbers of pseudorabies virus-labeled PC-INs individually at segments across cervical spinal cord, including separately in dorsal horn, intermediate gray, and ventral horn. We found that PC-INs are widespread throughout C1-C7 spinal cord in the uninjured condition. These PC-INs have a predominant intrasegmental connectivity pattern, though significant numbers of longer distance projecting propriospinal PC-INs also exist both rostral and caudal to the PhMN pool. Furthermore, while PC-INs connect both ipsilaterally and contralaterally, there is a strong bias to ipsilateral projection. C2 hemisection induced major disconnection between PhMNs and ipsilesional propriospinal PC-INs located rostral to the SCI, but induced more limited plasticity in connectivity of intrasegmental PC-INs located within C3-C6 spinal cord. These findings greatly improve our knowledge about PC-IN circuitry and also provide important information to aid in developing approaches to target PC-IN plasticity for promoting spinal cord repair.

title: Transient hippocampal CA1 responses follow the end of a treadmill delay during rat navigation.
abstract: The hippocampus is thought to organize experience in time, but how CA1 activity is structured around transitions between successive phases of behavior remains unclear.
